posts.title: You're Buying AI the Same Way You Bought Software in 2010. That's the Problem.
posts.content:
Let me describe a procurement process that probably feels familiar.

A business need gets identified. A requirements document gets written. Vendors get invited to pitch. The pitches happen—polished, confident, and full of impressive numbers and carefully selected case studies. A scoring matrix gets filled in. Legal reviews the contract. Finance signs off on the budget. The preferred vendor gets selected, and the engagement begins.

Clean. Structured. Defensible. The kind of process that looks exactly right in an audit.

And for most of the software your organization has bought over the last two decades, it worked. Not perfectly—no process is perfect—but well enough. The software did what the requirements said it should do. If it didn't, there was a contract clause about it. The relationship was transactional, and the expectations were clear.

The problem is that organizations are running that same process for AI. And AI is not software. Not in the ways that matter most when you're deciding whether to spend a significant portion of your technology budget on it.

And the gap between what that process was designed to evaluate and what AI actually is—is where a very large amount of money is currently disappearing.

What the old process was actually built for

To understand why traditional procurement breaks down with AI, it helps to be honest about what it was designed for in the first place.

Traditional software procurement assumes a few things that feel so obvious they rarely get stated explicitly.

It assumes the product is finished. The software exists. It does things. Those things are documented. You can evaluate whether the documented things match your requirements, and if they do, you buy it.

It assumes behavior is consistent and predictable. The software does the same thing every time, given the same input. If it doesn't, that's a bug—something to be fixed, not a fundamental characteristic of how the product works.

It assumes failure is binary and visible. Either the software works or it doesn't. Either the feature is there or it isn't. When something goes wrong, it's usually apparent. You can test for it. You can write contractual clauses around it.

And it assumes the vendor's job ends at delivery. You buy the software, it gets deployed, and the main ongoing relationship is about support—fixing things that break, updating things that change, and adding things that weren't in the original scope.

Every one of these assumptions breaks down with AI. Not partially. Fundamentally. And running a procurement process built on them produces a selection that looks rigorous from the outside and is deeply unreliable underneath.

Where it breaks down—specifically

Let me be concrete about this, because vague discomfort doesn't help anyone make better decisions.

The demo problem.

Traditional software demos show you the product. What you see is, more or less, what you get. The features are real. The interface is real. The behavior you're watching is the behavior you'll experience.

AI demos are different in a way that matters enormously. What you're watching is the system performing on data it has been optimized for, in conditions that have been carefully controlled, against use cases that have been specifically selected because they showcase the model's strengths.

That's not deception—it's how demos work. But with traditional software, the gap between demo conditions and production conditions is relatively small. With AI, it can be enormous. A model that performs brilliantly on curated demonstration data can fall apart on the messy, inconsistent, edge-case-heavy data that real business environments actually produce.

Traditional procurement has no good mechanism for evaluating this gap. The scoring matrix doesn't have a row for "how does this degrade under real-world conditions?" The requirements document doesn't capture "what happens when the input data doesn't look like the training set." And the evaluation panel—smart, experienced people—don't have the framework to ask those questions even when they sense they should.

So the best demo wins. Not the best solution.

The specification problem.

Traditional procurement is built around specifications. You define what you need. The vendor confirms they can deliver it. The contract captures the commitment. If what gets delivered doesn't match the specification, you have recourse.

AI doesn't lend itself to specification in that way. You can't write a requirement that says "the model shall correctly classify customer intent with 95% accuracy" the same way you'd write a requirement for a feature in a CRM system. Because that accuracy figure depends on the data, the use case, the edge cases, the distribution of inputs, and the definition of ""correct"—variables that are complex, context-dependent, and change over time.

So what happens in practice is one of two things. Either the specification stays vague—"the AI shall improve customer service outcomes"—which gives you no real basis for evaluating whether what gets delivered is good enough. Or it gets artificially precise—"95% accuracy"—without the understanding needed to know whether that number means what everyone assumes it means in the specific context of the organization's actual data and use cases.

Both versions fail. One fails obviously. The other fails quietly—and usually expensively.

The evaluation panel problem.

Traditional procurement evaluation panels are built for traditional procurement. They contain people who understand the business requirements, people who understand the technical architecture, and people who understand the commercial and legal implications.

What they almost never contain—because until recently there was no reason to—is someone who genuinely understands how AI systems behave. How they fail. What the difference is between a model that's technically performing and a model that's solving the right problem. What questions to ask a vendor that reveal real capability rather than presentation capability?

So the evaluation happens without the most important perspective in the room. And the vendor that presents most confidently, with the most polished materials and the most reassuring answers, gets selected. Not because the process is broken in theory. Because it's missing the expertise that would make it work in practice.

The contract problem.

Traditional software contracts are built around deliverables, timelines, and service levels. The software will be delivered by this date. It will have these features. It will maintain this uptime. If it doesn't, these remedies apply.

AI contracts need to capture something much more complex—and most legal teams don't yet have the frameworks to do it. How does performance get measured over time as data distributions shift? What happens when the model drifts—when accuracy that was acceptable at deployment has quietly degraded six months later? Who owns the liability when an AI system makes a decision that turns out to be wrong in a way that has real consequences for a customer or a regulator?

These are not hypothetical future questions. They are present, practical questions that AI deployments are already producing—and organizations that bought AI through a traditional contract structure are discovering, often at significant cost, that the contract they signed doesn't give them the protection they assumed it did.

The ongoing relationship problem.

Traditional software procurement treats the vendor relationship as largely transactional post-deployment. The software is deployed. Support is contracted. The main interaction is about fixes and updates.

AI is not a product you deploy and maintain. It's a system that needs active, ongoing stewardship. Models drift as the world changes around them. Data pipelines evolve. Edge cases multiply. Regulatory requirements shift. The system that was appropriate and accurate at deployment needs continuous attention—monitoring, evaluation, retraining, and recalibration—to stay appropriate and accurate over time.

Most AI procurement processes don't account for this. The budget covers the build and the initial deployment. The ongoing stewardship cost—which is real, significant, and not optional—lands as an unplanned operational expense that nobody allocated for, eating into the returns that were supposed to justify the investment.

What AI procurement actually needs to look like

Let me be clear that I'm not arguing for a more complicated process. Complexity for its own sake helps nobody. What I'm arguing for is a different process—one designed for what AI actually is rather than what we wish it were.

Start with the problem, not the technology.

The single most consistent mistake in AI procurement is starting with the solution. "We want to implement AI for customer service." That's a technology decision masquerading as a business decision. The right starting point is the specific, measurable business problem—and the question of whether AI is actually the best solution to it. Sometimes it is. Sometimes a better-designed process or a simpler automation would deliver more value with less risk. Starting with the problem rather than the technology changes the entire evaluation.

Evaluate on real data, not demo data.

Before any vendor gets serious consideration, they should be evaluated on a representative sample of your actual data—not their curated demonstration set. What does the model do when it encounters the edge cases that are specific to your business? How does performance degrade when the input data is messier than the training set? This evaluation will be imperfect — no sample is perfectly representative — but it will reveal things that no demo ever will.

Add AI fluency to the evaluation panel.

Every AI procurement evaluation needs someone who understands how AI systems actually behave—their failure modes, their limitations, and the questions that reveal real capability versus presentation capability. This doesn't need to be the most technical person in the organization. It needs to be someone with enough genuine AI fluency to catch the things that an experienced but AI-unfamiliar evaluation panel will miss.

Build ongoing performance into the contract.

The contract shouldn't just capture what gets delivered at deployment. It should define how performance gets measured over time, what happens when it degrades, who carries the responsibility for monitoring and maintaining accuracy, and what the remedies are when the system fails to perform against the agreed baseline. These are harder conversations to have before the contract is signed. They are considerably harder to have afterward.

Budget for the full lifecycle—honestly.

The build cost is the visible cost. The ongoing stewardship cost—monitoring, maintenance, retraining, regulatory compliance, performance management—is the invisible one. Any AI budget that doesn't explicitly account for the full lifecycle cost is not a real budget. It's a down payment with deferred surprises attached.

The questions worth asking before the next vendor conversation

Before the next AI vendor pitch, before the next evaluation panel meets, before the next contract goes to legal—try these:

→ Are we evaluating this vendor on our data or theirs?
→ Does our evaluation panel include someone who genuinely understands how AI fails?
→ Have we defined success in terms that we can actually measure over time—not just at deployment?
→ Does our contract capture ongoing performance obligations—not just delivery?
→ Have we budgeted honestly for the full lifecycle—including the costs that don't appear in the vendor's proposal?

If any of those questions feel hard to answer, that's where to focus before the conversation goes any further.

The Monday Reality Check

The procurement process your organization uses for AI was designed for a different kind of technology. It was built for products that do what they say, behave consistently, and can be evaluated against fixed specifications. It was built for a transactional vendor relationship where the main ongoing obligation is support.

AI is none of those things. And running it through a process designed for something else produces selections that look defensible on paper and are quietly unreliable in practice. Vendors that present well over vendors that perform well. Contracts that protect against the wrong risks. Budgets that cover the visible costs and ignore the real ones.

The fix doesn't require reinventing procurement from scratch. It requires being honest about what AI is, what evaluating it properly demands, and what the process needs to look like to produce decisions you can actually stand behind eighteen months later when the deployment is live and the real conditions are nothing like the demo.

Your procurement process is one of the most important decisions you make about AI—because it determines everything that comes after it.

It's worth getting right.

Have you been through an AI procurement process that felt off—where the evaluation didn't quite capture what mattered? What would you do differently? I'd genuinely like to hear.

posts.title: Your AI Project Doesn’t Have an AI Problem. It Has a Manager Problem.
posts.content:
Let me tell you about a situation that’s playing out in organizations everywhere right now—and almost nobody is naming it, honestly.

An AI initiative gets approved. The budget is there. Leadership picks someone to run it—someone good. Someone who’s delivered before, navigated complexity before, and earned the organization's trust over years of solid work. Someone everyone genuinely believes can handle it.

And then things start going sideways.

Not dramatically. Not all at once. Just a slow, quiet accumulation of things that don’t quite add up. Timelines that keep slipping by just enough to seem manageable. Vendor conversations that produce more questions than answers. A technical team and a business team that seem to be talking about two completely different projects without either side fully realizing it. Decisions that should take days, taking weeks. Scope that keeps expanding without anyone being able to explain exactly why.

And then, around the six-month mark, there’s that feeling. The one nobody wants to say out loud in the status meeting. That something fundamental isn’t working—and the gap between what was promised and what’s actually happening is starting to get hard to paper over.

So the investigation begins. Leadership looks at the technology. Looks at the vendor. Looks at the timeline and the budget. And eventually, if they’re honest, they look at the person running it.

What almost nobody looks at is the decision to put that person in that role—without giving them what they actually needed to succeed.

That’s what I want to talk about today.

The logic that feels completely sound—until it isn't.
I want to start here, because I think it’s important to understand why organizations keep making this call—and why it keeps feeling like the right one at the time.

The manager they picked is genuinely good. They know the business inside out. They know how to handle stakeholders, how to navigate internal politics, and how to keep a complex project moving when it starts to stall. They’ve delivered before, in difficult conditions, against real pressure. There’s a track record there. There’s trust.

And on the surface, AI projects look like complex projects. They have budgets and timelines and vendors and deliverables and stakeholders pulling in different directions. They need someone who can coordinate across functions, manage expectations upward, and make decisions under uncertainty.

So the experienced manager gets the role. Or the operations director who led the last digital transformation. Or the department head who’s engaged with the AI conversation and seems genuinely interested in making it work.

And the assumption—rarely said out loud, but almost always sitting underneath the decision—is that the technical complexity will be handled by the technical people, and the manager will handle the management.

That assumption is where everything quietly starts to go wrong.

What nobody tells them
Here’s the thing about handing an AI project to someone without a real framework for how AI works.

They manage it like a technology project. And AI is not a technology project. Not really. Not in the ways that matter most at the project management level.

In a traditional technology project, you can define requirements upfront with reasonable precision. The system either does what it was designed to do or it doesn’t. Success and failure are relatively clear. The main risks are delivery risks—timeline, budget, scope, and integration.

AI doesn’t behave that way. And the differences are not minor technical footnotes. They’re fundamental—and they show up in the decisions a project owner makes every single week.

AI systems are probabilistic. They don’t always do the same thing twice. A model can be technically working and practically useless at the same time. It can be ninety percent accurate overall and catastrophically wrong in the specific ten percent of cases that matter most to the business. It can perform beautifully on the data it was trained on and fall apart on the data it actually encounters in production.

A manager without a framework for understanding this will make decisions that look reasonable from the outside and are quietly damaging underneath. And they’ll make them confidently—because they don’t know what they don’t know.

Let me show you exactly where this plays out.

Vendor selection—where the best presenter wins
A non-technical manager sitting across the table from an AI vendor is, whether they realize it or not, almost entirely dependent on what the vendor chooses to tell them.

And vendors—understandably, this is their job—present their technology in the most compelling light they can. The demos are polished. The case studies are carefully curated. The capability claims are technically accurate in the right conditions, with the right data, under controlled circumstances.

Without a framework for asking the questions that actually matter—what happens when the data doesn’t look like your training set? How does performance degrade under real-world conditions? What does the monitoring requirement look like eighteen months post-deployment? What are the failure modes we should be planning for? — the evaluation defaults to what’s always defaulted to when people don’t have the tools to evaluate properly.

Relationship. Presentation quality. The comfort of a confident answer.

The best presenter wins. Not the best solution. And by the time the gap between the demo and the reality becomes visible, the contract is signed and the clock is ticking.

Defining success—with words that sound right but mean nothing
Here’s a small but devastating thing that happens on almost every AI project managed this way.

Success gets defined in language that sounds reasonable and is almost impossible to evaluate honestly.

“The AI should improve our customer experience.”
"The system should make our operations more efficient.”
"We want AI to help our team make better decisions.”

These are not success criteria. They are intentions dressed up as outcomes. And the problem with intentions is that they’re almost impossible to fail against—which means the project can run for months, consuming budget and resource and goodwill, without anyone being able to say clearly whether it’s working or not.

Proper AI success criteria look different. They’re specific. They’re measurable in ways that reflect how AI actually behaves. They’re defined before the work starts—not reverse-engineered afterward to fit whatever the system turned out to be capable of.

A manager without the framework to know this will accept vague success criteria—not because they’re being careless, but because nobody told them the vagueness was the problem.

Managing the technical team—the gap that does the most damage
This is the one I find most difficult to watch, because it does the most quiet, sustained damage—to the project, to the team, and often to the manager personally.

Write on Medium
When there’s a significant asymmetry of understanding between a manager and their technical team, two things tend to happen. Neither of them is good.

The technical team stops surfacing problems early. Not because they’re being difficult. Because experience has taught them that surfacing problems early leads to pressure they can’t explain their way out of from someone who doesn’t have the context to distinguish between a solvable challenge and a fundamental architectural issue. So problems get managed internally, worked around, and quietly absorbed—until they’re too big to hide. At which point they’ve become considerably more expensive than they would have been if someone had caught them three months earlier.

And the manager—sensing that they don’t fully understand what’s happening underneath them and feeling the pressure from leadership above them—does one of two things. They defer too much to the technical team and lose the visibility they need to make good decisions. Or they push too hard on timelines and deliverables—applying the same pressure that works on traditional projects—and get shortcuts in return. Workarounds that look like progress. A system that launches on time and underperforms in production for the next eighteen months.

Both dynamics are completely understandable. And both are entirely predictable when you put someone in a role without the framework the role demands.

The moment everything comes apart
There’s almost always a specific moment—usually somewhere between month three and month five—where the gap between what was promised and what’s actually happening becomes impossible to manage quietly.

The pilot results are underwhelming. The technical team is raising concerns about the data architecture that weren’t visible at the start. The vendor is explaining, apologetically, why the original timeline needs to move. And the manager is caught between a technical reality they can’t fully interpret and a leadership team that was sold a different story.

In that moment, without the right framework, there are really only two moves available.

Apply pressure. Push the team and the vendor to hit the original commitments anyway. Which produces a system that launches on schedule and quietly fails to deliver in production—where the real conditions are nothing like the controlled environment the timeline was built around.

Or escalate without sufficient diagnosis. Go to leadership with a problem that can’t be properly explained, which produces the wrong kind of intervention at the wrong moment. The project gets restructured, or shut down, or handed to someone else—and the capable, trusted manager who was put in an impossible position walks away with a damaged reputation they didn’t deserve.

Neither outcome is the manager’s fault. The fault belongs upstream—to the decision that placed them there without the support structure the role actually required.

What good AI project ownership actually looks like
Let me be clear about what I’m not saying here.

I’m not saying only technical people can lead AI projects. That’s not true, and it would miss the point entirely. Some of the most effective AI project owners are not technical at all—in the conventional sense.

What they have, instead of technical depth, is something more valuable for the role they’re in: genuine AI fluency. A real framework for understanding how these systems behave, where they tend to fail, what questions to ask at each stage, and how to tell the difference between a problem that needs more time and a problem that needs a fundamentally different approach.

That fluency is not a personality trait. It’s not something people either have or don’t have. It’s learnable—through education, through deliberate exposure, and through building enough understanding to have the right conversations even when you’re not the most technical person in the room.

A project owner with genuine AI fluency knows how to ask vendors the questions that reveal real capability rather than demo capability. They know how to define success criteria that reflect how AI actually behaves. They know how to create an environment where the technical team surfaces problems early rather than managing them quietly. They know when to push and when the push itself is the problem.

They don’t need to build the system. They need to understand it well enough to make good decisions about it. Consistently. Under pressure. When the gap between the plan and the reality is starting to show.

That’s the standard. And it’s the standard organizations need to be explicit about before the project gets assigned—not discovered halfway through when things have already started to unravel.

What leadership needs to own
If you’ve assigned a capable, trusted person to an AI initiative—I'm not suggesting you made the wrong call on the person.

I’m suggesting you may have made an incomplete call on what they needed around them to succeed.

Before the next project gets assigned, sit with these honestly:

Does this person have a genuine framework for AI—not just project management experience?

Have we invested in building that framework—or are we assuming it transfers from other kinds of complexity?

Are there success criteria defined in terms that reflect how AI actually behaves—not just what we hope it will do?

Is there a technically fluent advisor built into the project structure—not to take over, but to give the project owner the context they need at the moments that matter?

Because the honest truth underneath all of this is simple.

Putting a good person in a role they weren’t equipped for and then being disappointed when they struggle is not a talent problem.

It’s a leadership problem.

Here’s where I’ll leave you this Monday.
AI projects don’t fail because the technology doesn’t work.

They fail because the person responsible for them was handed authority without the framework to use it well. Because the organization assumed that being good at managing complexity automatically translates to being equipped for this specific kind of complexity. Because the mismatch between what the role actually demanded and what the person was set up with was visible from the start—and nobody said anything.

The fix is not complicated. It’s not expensive. It just requires honesty—about what AI project ownership actually demands and what it takes to give someone a genuine chance of delivering it.

Stop handing good people impossible positions.

Give them the framework. Give them the right support structure. Give them an honest picture of what they’re walking into.

And if you’re not sure you can do that before the project starts—

that uncertainty is worth sitting with before you make the call.

Have you seen this play out—a capable person handed an AI project without the right support around them? What happened? I’d genuinely like to hear.

posts.title: Your AI Budget Looks Healthy. Your AI ROI Doesn’t. Here’s the Gap Nobody’s Talking About.
posts.content:
Let me ask you something that might feel a little uncomfortable.

When was the last time someone in your organization sat down—honestly, without the quarterly narrative, without the innovation story, without the competitive pressure framing the conversation—and asked what you’re actually getting back from your AI spend?

Not what the dashboard says. Not what the vendor reported. Not the adoption rate or the prompts run or the number of teams that have “gone live.”

What is the business actually getting back?

If that question made you pause—even slightly—you're not alone. And the pause itself is worth paying attention to.

The budget feels like progress. Sometimes it isn’t.
Here’s something that doesn’t get said in enough boardrooms right now.

Having a healthy AI budget and having a healthy AI return are two completely different things. And somewhere along the way—quietly, gradually, with the best of intentions on everyone’s side—a lot of organizations have started treating the first as evidence of the second.

The budget grows. The spend feels justified. The competitive pressure makes any AI investment feel like the responsible move. And the question of what’s actually coming back gets softer and vaguer with each passing quarter—not because nobody cares, but because the honest answer is murkier than anyone wants to put in a board presentation.

So the budget stays healthy. The ROI conversation stays comfortable. And the gap between the two keeps quietly widening.

I understand why this happens. The psychology of AI investment right now is genuinely unusual. In most areas of business spending, the burden of proof is clear—you show the expected return, you get the budget, and if the return doesn’t materialize, the investment gets scrutinized.

AI has somehow flipped that. The implicit logic running through most boardrooms right now is something like: the cost of being left behind is unknowable and potentially catastrophic, so any AI investment is defensible because at least we’re moving.

That logic isn’t completely wrong. But it’s created an environment where budgets get approved on competitive anxiety rather than financial rigor. Where the normal discipline around return on investment gets quietly suspended in the name of innovation. Where activity gets reported as progress because progress is harder to measure.

And nobody says this out loud. Which is exactly why it keeps happening.

Where the money is actually going
Let me be specific, because vague discomfort isn’t useful. Here’s where the AI budget quietly disappears in most organizations—and why it’s so easy to miss until the numbers become impossible to ignore.

The tool sprawl nobody noticed.

At some point, AI procurement became everyone’s job. Marketing bought a tool. Sales bought a tool. Operations bought one. HR bought one. Each purchase was individually justified, individually approved, and individually reported upward as progress.

Nobody added them up. Nobody checked whether they talked to each other. Nobody asked whether the problems they were each solving were actually connected to something that mattered at the organizational level.

What you end up with is a portfolio that looks impressive in aggregate and delivers less than the sum of its parts. Licenses are sitting at low utilization. Overlapping capabilities nobody noticed because nobody looked across the whole picture. Integration costs that were never budgeted because nobody planned for integration at the point of purchase.

Each individual decision made sense. The pattern only becomes visible when someone looks at the whole thing—and in most organizations, that moment keeps getting deferred.

The pilot that looked like proof.

A pilot gets funded. Controlled environment, carefully selected use case, extra attention, and resources. It works. The demo is genuinely impressive. The project gets the green light for the next phase.

And then the next phase hits the real world. The data outside the controlled environment is messier. The edge cases multiply faster than anyone expected. The integration with existing systems turns out to be three times more complicated than the original estimate. The timeline extends. The budget grows. And gradually, almost without anyone deciding it, the “scaling” phase starts consuming more than the pilot ever did—without producing proportionally more value.

This isn’t the technology failing. It’s what happens when pilots are designed to demonstrate rather than to stress-test. A pilot that doesn’t specifically surface the obstacles to scaling isn’t a proof of concept. It’s a very expensive demo with good lighting.

The maintenance bill nobody budgeted for.

This one quietly catches almost everyone.

AI systems are not static. Models drift as the world around them changes. Data pipelines need ongoing attention. Edge cases that never appeared in testing start appearing in production six months later. Regulatory requirements shift. The system that was accurate and reliable at launch needs real, sustained effort to stay accurate and reliable.

None of this is a surprise to anyone who’s actually built these systems. But it’s almost always missing from the business cases that get AI projects approved—because business cases are built to get projects funded, and ongoing maintenance costs have a way of making the numbers look less compelling.

So the budget covers the build. The cost of keeping it working properly shows up later as an unplanned operational expense—quietly eating into the returns that were supposed to justify the whole thing.

The measurement problem that makes everything worse
Here’s where I want to get practical, because this is the part that’s actually fixable—if leadership decides to fix it.

Most organizations are measuring AI activity. Prompts run. Tools deployed. Adoption rates. Training hours completed. These numbers are easy to produce, easy to present, and almost completely useless as indicators of whether the investment is working.

Activity metrics tell you things are happening.
Outcome metrics tell you whether what’s happening is making a difference.

And the shift from one to the other requires something that most AI projects skip—defining the outcome before the project starts, not after it needs to be reported.

Here’s what that actually looks like in practice.

Instead of "How many people are using the tool?"—ask", "What specific decision or action is this tool supposed to improve, and is it improving it?”

Instead of asking, "What's our adoption rate?" ask, "What can people do now that they couldn’t do six months ago, and is that showing up in the results?”

Instead of "How many AI projects are live?" ask", "Which of those projects is producing a measurable return, and what’s the honest plan for the ones that aren’t?”

These are harder questions. They require more rigor, more honesty, and more willingness to sit with answers that aren’t comfortable. They’re also the only questions that tell you whether the budget is doing what a budget is supposed to do.

What good actually looks like
I want to be clear that this isn’t an argument against investing in AI. It’s an argument for investing in it with more clarity and more accountability.

The AI investments that genuinely deliver — and there are plenty of them — tend to share a few things in common.

They start with a specific, measurable problem. Not “we want to improve customer service with AI.” Something more like "We want to reduce tier-one query resolution time from four hours to under one hour, without increasing headcount.” Specific. Measurable. Connected to something the business actually cares about.

They define what success looks like before the money moves. What does good look like in six months? In twelve? What would need to be true for this to have been worth it? These questions get answered at the start—not reverse-engineered at the end to fit the numbers.

They build measurement from day one. The infrastructure to track the outcome exists before the AI goes live. The return gets measured against a real baseline, not estimated after the fact with generous assumptions.

And—this one matters more than people admit—they have an honest plan for what happens if it doesn’t work. Not every AI investment will deliver. The ones that recover well are the ones where leadership already thought about the early warning signs, the decision criteria for changing course, and how to do that without it becoming a political problem.

Sit with these this week.
Before the next budget review. Before the next AI project gets approved. Before the next quarterly update shows healthy spending and a comfortable narrative:

→ Can you name the specific business outcome each current AI investment is supposed to move—and point to data that shows whether it’s actually moving?
→ When did you last look at your AI tool portfolio as a whole—utilization, overlap, total cost, integration debt?
→ Are you measuring activity or outcomes—and would you know the difference if someone pushed you on it in a board meeting?
→ What percentage of your AI budget is going to maintenance versus new capability—and is that ratio something you chose or something that just happened?

Here’s where I’ll leave you this Monday.
A healthy AI budget is not a strategy.

It’s a starting point. And right now, for a lot of organizations, it’s a starting point that’s quietly becoming an endpoint—because the hard conversation about what’s actually coming back keeps getting deferred in favor of the more comfortable conversation about what’s being spent.

The organizations that look back on this period with confidence won’t be the ones that spent the most. They’ll be the ones that spent with the most clarity—that knew what they were trying to change, measured whether it changed, and had the honesty to act on what the numbers actually said.

That gap between budget and return won’t close by itself.

But it closes fast the moment someone in the room decides to stop asking, "How much are we spending on AI?” and starts asking, "What are we actually getting back—and how do we know?”

Be that person. This Monday.

When did you last have a genuinely honest conversation about AI ROI in your organization—not the reported version, but the real one? I’d genuinely like to hear what that conversation looked like.

posts.title: You hired an AI consultancy. Now You’re Dependent on Them Forever. Here’s why.
posts.content:
Let me start with a scenario that might feel a little close to home.

Eighteen months ago, the pressure to do something meaningful with AI reached a tipping point. The board was asking questions. Competitors were making moves. Internal capability wasn’t there yet—and honestly, the timeline to build it felt too long. So the organization did what smart organizations do when they need to move fast in unfamiliar territory.

They hired a consultancy.

Good one, too. Sharp people, impressive credentials, and a client list that inspired confidence. The engagement kicked off with a discovery phase, then a strategy phase, then an implementation phase. Deliverables came in on time. The demos looked great. Leadership felt, for the first time in a while, like the organization was genuinely moving forward on AI.

And then, quietly, something started to feel off.

Every time a question came up about the system — how it worked, why it made a particular decision, how to adjust it as the business evolved — the answer was the same: we’ll need to loop in the consultancy on that one.

Every enhancement, every integration, every piece of maintenance—the consultancy. Every time something broke, something drifted, or something needed rethinking—the consultancy.

Twelve months after the engagement was supposed to end, the contract was still running. The budget line that was meant to be temporary had quietly become permanent. And somewhere along the way, without anyone quite deciding it, the consultancy had become load-bearing infrastructure.

This is the consultant trap. And it’s happening in organisations everywhere right now — not because anyone planned it that way, but because the incentive structures involved make it almost inevitable when nobody’s paying close enough attention.

Why it happens — and why it’s not entirely the consultancy’s fault
I want to be careful here, because the easy version of this story is that consultancies are deliberately engineering dependency to protect their revenue. And sometimes that’s true. But more often, the dynamic is subtler and more structural than that — and understanding it properly is the only way to protect yourself from it.

Consultancies are optimised to deliver outcomes. That’s what they’re hired for, that’s what they’re measured on, and that’s what their model is built around. When you engage a consultancy to build an AI system, they will build you an AI system. They’ll build it well, they’ll deliver it on time, and they’ll make sure it works.

What they are almost never explicitly hired to do is transfer the deep understanding of that system into your organisation. Not the surface-level understanding — how to use the dashboard, how to interpret the outputs. The real understanding. Why the architecture was designed the way it was. What assumptions are baked into the model. What breaks first when the business context shifts. How to evolve the system as the organisation’s needs evolve.

That knowledge lives with the people who built it. And those people work for the consultancy.

So when the engagement ends and the consultancy leaves, they take that knowledge with them. Your organisation has the system, the documentation, and the training sessions. But it doesn’t have the understanding. And without the understanding, it can’t maintain the system independently, it can’t evolve it intelligently, and it can’t make good decisions about what to build next.

Which means the next time something needs to happen — and something always needs to happen — you call the consultancy.

What dependency actually looks like
The tricky thing about the consultant trap is that it doesn’t feel like a trap while you’re in it. It feels like a sensible ongoing relationship with a trusted partner. The warning signs are easy to rationalise away.

Here’s what to look for.

Your internal team can describe what the system does but not how it works. They can walk you through the outputs and the dashboard and the workflow. But ask them why the model weights certain signals more heavily than others, or what happens to the predictions when market conditions shift significantly, and the answer trails off into uncertainty. That gap — between using the system and understanding it — is where dependency lives.

Every non-routine question goes back to the consultancy. Routine operations run fine internally. But anything that requires judgment — a new integration, a performance issue, a question about whether the system is still calibrated correctly as the business has evolved — gets escalated externally. If your consultancy is the decision-maker for anything beyond basic operation, you don’t own the system. You rent it.

The original engagement keeps extending. This one sounds obvious but it’s surprisingly easy to miss in the moment, because each extension feels individually justified. There’s a new requirement. There’s a performance issue that needs addressing. There’s an integration that wasn’t in the original scope. Each extension is reasonable. The pattern of extensions is a signal worth paying attention to.

Nobody internally could rebuild it if they had to. This is the cleanest test. If the consultancy disappeared tomorrow — contract ended, company acquired, key people moved on — could your internal team keep the system running, diagnose problems, and make intelligent decisions about its evolution? If the honest answer is no, you’re dependent. Full stop.

The difference between a consultancy that builds your capability and one that replaces it
Not all consultancy relationships become traps. Some of the best AI implementations I’ve seen were delivered by external partners — because the engagement was structured deliberately to transfer capability, not just deliver output.

The difference comes down to one question, and it’s worth asking it explicitly before you sign anything:

Is this engagement designed to make us less dependent on you over time or more?

A consultancy that builds your capability embeds with your internal team rather than working alongside them. They pair external expertise with internal people from day one—not to make the project run smoother, but to make sure the knowledge doesn’t leave when they do. They document decisions, not just outcomes—explaining why the architecture was designed a particular way, what trade-offs were made, and what would need to be revisited if the business context changed. They define success partly as internal capability—not just a working system, but a team that genuinely understands what they’ve been given.

A consultancy that replaces your capability does the opposite. They work in a way that’s efficient for them rather than educational for you. The documentation covers what the system does but not why. The handover is a presentation and a set of credentials, not a genuine transfer of understanding. And the measure of success is a functioning deliverable—with no explicit commitment to what your organization can do independently on the other side of it.

Both types of engagement can produce excellent systems. Only one of them leaves you in a stronger position than when you started.

What leadership needs to do differently
This is where I want to be direct, because the consultant trap is ultimately a leadership problem—not a consultancy problem.

Consultancies will structure engagements the way their clients allow them to be structured. If nobody pushes for capability transfer, capability transfer won’t happen. If the success metrics are all about the system and none of them are about internal understanding, internal understanding won’t be prioritized. If leadership doesn’t ask the hard questions at the start of the engagement, they’ll be living with the answers at the end of it.

So here’s what to do differently.

Before you sign, ask explicitly how the engagement builds internal capability. Not as an afterthought. As a core requirement. If the answer is vague or treats it as a nice-to-have rather than a structural part of the engagement, that tells you something important.

Insist on pairing. Every significant piece of work done by the consultancy should have an internal counterpart learning alongside it. Not observing—participating. This slows things down slightly and costs more in internal time. It’s worth it.

Make knowledge transfer a contractual deliverable. Not documentation—understanding. The test isn’t whether the consultancy produced a technical document. It’s whether your internal team can answer questions about the system that they couldn’t answer before the engagement started.

Define your exit clearly at the start. What does a successful handover look like? What can your internal team do independently at the end of this engagement that they can’t do now? If you can’t answer these questions before the work begins, you’re not ready to start the work.

The question worth sitting with this week
If you’re currently in a consultancy engagement—or about to enter one—here's the honest question to take into your next conversation with them:

If this engagement ended tomorrow, what could we do independently that we couldn’t do before you arrived?

If the answer is primarily about the system they’ve built rather than the capability they’ve transferred, you’re building a dependency, not an advantage.

And dependencies, in AI, are expensive. They compound quietly. And by the time most organizations notice how deep they go, unpicking them costs considerably more than building the internal capability would have from the start.

The Monday Reality Check
Hiring a consultancy to accelerate your AI journey is not the problem. Done well, it’s one of the smartest moves a leadership team can make.

The problem is hiring a consultancy as a substitute for building internal capability—and then being surprised when, twelve months later, you can’t do anything meaningful with AI without picking up the phone to someone outside your organization.

You don’t need to own every piece of your AI infrastructure. But you do need to understand it. You do need internal people who can make intelligent decisions about it. And you do need an engagement model that leaves your organization stronger, not more dependent, than when it started.

The goal was never to have a great AI system.

The goal was to become an organization that can build, run, and evolve great AI systems.

Those are very different destinations. And which one you end up at depends almost entirely on the questions you ask before the work begins.

Have you found yourself deeper in a consultancy dependency than you planned? What did you do about it? I’d genuinely like to hear.

posts.title: AI Transformation Doesn’t Fail at the Top. It Dies in the Middle.
posts.content:
Let me paint you a picture that might feel uncomfortably familiar.

The CEO just came back from a conference. Eyes lit up, energy high, head full of possibilities. Within a week, there’s a strategy session. Within a month, there’s a budget. Within a quarter, there’s a roadmap, a rollout plan, and an internal announcement that goes out to the whole organization under the subject line "Our AI Journey Starts Now.”

Everyone claps. Or at least, everyone hits the thumbs up on the company intranet.

And then—slowly, quietly, without anyone quite meaning for it to happen—nothing much changes.

The tools get purchased. The licenses get activated. The training sessions get scheduled, and some of them even get attended. But six months later, if you walk the floors and have honest conversations with the people doing the actual work, you find that the AI initiative that looked so promising in the boardroom has somehow lost its pulse somewhere between the vision and the reality.

The technology works fine. The strategy made sense. The budget was there.

So what happened?

I’ll tell you what happened. And I’ll be direct about it, because this particular truth tends to get softened into uselessness every time someone tries to say it politely.

It died in the middle.

The layer nobody talks about
Here’s the dynamic that plays out in organization after organization and almost never gets named at the board level until it’s too late.

The top is genuinely bought in. The CEO means it. The leadership team means it. The vision is real, the commitment is real, and the investment is real.

The frontline—the people doing the day-to-day work—are actually more adaptable than anyone gives them credit for. Give someone a tool that makes their Thursday afternoon less painful and they’ll figure it out. People are remarkably good at embracing things that genuinely help them.

But the middle — the operations managers, the department heads, the team leads, the people who sit between the boardroom’s vision and the frontline’s reality — that’s where everything slows down. That’s where the urgency softens. That’s where “we’re still evaluating the best approach for our team” becomes a permanent state of being.

And here’s the painful part. Leadership usually doesn’t see it happening in real time. What they see is adoption metrics and progress reports and pilot updates. What they don’t see is the quiet culture forming underneath — the eye-rolls in the team meeting, the “we tried that and it didn’t really work for us” conversations spreading through the organisation like a slow leak, the workarounds that spring up because the tool technically exists but nobody is using it the way it was intended.

By the time that culture is visible at the board level, it’s already embedded. And embedded resistance is a completely different — and much harder — problem than early resistance.

Let’s talk about why — because the reason matters
This is the part of the conversation that tends to make people uncomfortable. So I’m going to say it plainly, without the usual corporate cushioning.

Middle managers are not resisting AI because they’re stuck in the past or afraid of change or fundamentally opposed to progress. They’re resisting it because, from where they’re sitting, it looks like a very real threat to something they’ve spent years building.

Their expertise. Their authority. Their value to the organisation.

Think about what AI actually does when it’s working properly. It automates the judgment calls that used to require experience. It surfaces insights that used to require a skilled person to interpret. It compresses timelines that used to require coordination, oversight, and someone in the middle making sure everything connected properly.

All of the things a good middle manager does—now potentially running inside a system that doesn’t need a salary or a performance review or a one-to-one every fortnight.

So when the all-hands meeting announces that AI is the company’s biggest strategic priority this year, what a middle manager hears underneath the optimism and the roadmap slides is a much more personal question: where do I fit in this new world?

And until that question gets a direct and honest answer, the rational move — the completely human and understandable move — is to protect what you have. To move slowly. To be technically compliant without being genuinely committed. To do enough to avoid friction with leadership while making sure nothing changes too fast, too close to home.

This isn’t sabotage. It’s self-preservation. And if leadership hasn’t given people a reason to feel secure, they have no right to be surprised by it.

The silence that makes everything worse
Here’s where I want to be genuinely direct, because I think this is where most organizations are getting it badly wrong right now.

The silence around this problem is a choice. And it’s an expensive one.

Most AI transformation programs are detailed, rigorous, and well-funded on the technology side. The tool selection is thorough. The implementation plan is careful. The vendor relationships are managed properly.

And the human side? The people side? The “how do we actually bring the layer of our organization that makes everything happen along with us” side?

That usually gets a two-hour change management workshop and an FAQ document.

That imbalance is not a technology failure. It’s a leadership failure. And it won’t fix itself while everyone politely avoids naming it.

The organizations genuinely winning at AI transformation right now are not the ones with the most sophisticated technology stack. They’re the ones that treated the human dimension of the change with the same rigor and seriousness as the technical dimension. They’re the ones that had the uncomfortable conversations early—about roles, about job security, about what will genuinely change and what won't—instead of hoping those conversations would become unnecessary as things progressed.

Spoiler: they never become unnecessary. They just get harder the longer you leave them.

What actually fixes this?
The good news—and there is genuine good news here—is that this problem is solvable. It doesn’t require a new strategy or a bigger budget or a different technology. It requires a different approach to the people in the middle of this change.

Bring them into the design, not just the deployment.

The most consistent mistake in AI transformation is treating middle management as an implementation channel—a pipe through which the boardroom’s decisions flow down to the frontline. But these are the people who understand, better than anyone in the leadership team, how work actually gets done inside the organization. They know which processes are genuinely followed versus theoretically followed. They know where the real friction is. They know where AI could genuinely help versus where it would just add a new layer of complexity to an already complicated situation.

Involve them properly—not as a consultation exercise that happens after the decisions have already been made, but as genuine participants in figuring out what good looks like. You’ll get better implementations. And you’ll get people who feel ownership over the outcome rather than obligation to comply with someone else’s vision.

Answer the question they’re actually asking.

Every middle manager sitting through an AI strategy presentation is asking a version of the same question internally: what does this mean for me, specifically?

Not for the company. Not for the industry. For them. Their role. Their team. Their future in this organization.

Until that question gets a real answer—not corporate reassurance language about “evolving skill sets” and “exciting new opportunities,” but an actual, honest conversation about what changes and what doesn't—everything else lands on deaf ears. Because humans are very good at not hearing things that feel like they’re avoiding the question they actually care about.

Have the direct conversation. It’s uncomfortable. Have it anyway. The discomfort of one honest conversation is considerably smaller than the cost of an AI transformation that quietly stalls because nobody wanted to say the hard thing.

Change the metrics before you change the behavior.

A lot of middle manager resistance—and this is something that almost never gets discussed—comes from a very simple structural problem. The metrics they’re being measured on haven’t changed. But the way work is supposed to get done has.

So you’re asking people to adopt new tools and new approaches while still being evaluated on the same KPIs that existed before any of this started. That’s a conflict. And when humans face a conflict between doing the new thing and hitting their numbers, they hit their numbers. Every time. It’s not a character flaw. It’s just how incentive structures work.

If AI genuinely changes how work gets done, the measures of good performance need to reflect that. Define what great looks like in an AI-augmented environment—and communicate it clearly, before asking people to change how they work.

One question for this week
If you’re leading an AI transformation that isn’t quite moving the way you hoped—and you’re being honest with yourself about it—here's the only question that matters right now:

When did you last have a real conversation with someone in your middle layer about how they actually feel about what’s happening?

Not a town hall. Not a survey. A real conversation, with a real person, about the real friction. The kind of conversation where you listen more than you talk, and you resist the urge to immediately reassure.

If the answer is “not recently," that’s where you start. Not with a new vendor. Not with a revised rollout timeline. With a conversation that’s probably overdue.

Here’s the reality check.
AI transformation doesn’t fail because the technology isn’t ready.

It fails because organizations treat a fundamentally human challenge as if it were a technical one—and then express genuine surprise when the humans don’t behave like the implementation plan assumed they would.

The boardroom declared the transformation. The strategy is set. The budget is approved. The technology is ready.

Now comes the harder part—actually leading the people in the middle of your organization through a change that feels uncertain and threatening, with enough honesty and enough humanity that they choose to move with you rather than quietly around you.

That’s not an AI problem. That’s a leadership problem.

And it’s yours to solve.

Have you seen this play out—the quiet resistance that nobody names until it’s already embedded? What finally broke the deadlock? I’d genuinely like to hear it.
