posts.title: Moving Fast With AI Isn’t the Advantage Everyone Thinks It Is
posts.content:
There’s a pattern showing up in boardrooms right now that nobody is talking about openly.

Not failure, exactly. Not success either. Something murkier and more uncomfortable than both—organizations that have moved fast on AI, spent real money, made real announcements, and are now sitting quietly with the gap between what they expected and what they actually got.
Four tools deployed. Three departments involved. Eight weeks of activity. And when you ask how it’s going, there’s a pause. The kind of pause that says more than the answer that follows.
"We’re still figuring out what we actually got."
That pause is where I want to start today. Because I think it’s more honest than most of the AI conversation happening right now—and I think it points at something important about the moment we’re in.

The pressure is real—let's acknowledge that first.
I’m not here to be dismissive about why this happens. The pressure to move fast on AI right now is coming from multiple directions at once, and it’s genuinely hard to resist.
Competitors are making announcements. Board members are asking pointed questions in quarterly reviews. Vendors are running compelling demos. The financial press is publishing a new "AI changes everything" piece roughly every 48 hours. And somewhere in the middle of all that noise, leadership teams are trying to make sensible decisions with incomplete information and a calendar that was already full before any of this started.
So when I say organizations are moving too fast, I’m not saying they’re being reckless. I’m saying they’re responding rationally to irrational pressure. And that’s a meaningfully different problem—because it means the solution isn’t better judgment. It’s better framing.
The question worth asking isn’t "how do we move faster?"
It’s "What are we actually racing towards, and is speed the right vehicle to get there?"

What does "fast" actually look like in practice?
Here’s the pattern that’s playing out right now across industries.
A leadership team feels the heat. Competitors are announcing AI initiatives. The board is asking why the organization isn’t further along. Someone in the room says—reasonably—that they need to stop talking about it and start doing something. Tools get selected. Pilots get launched. A press release goes out. The internal newsletter celebrates a new chapter.
And then, quietly, reality starts to show up.
The AI tool that was supposed to save the customer service team ten hours a week is generating responses that someone still needs to check before they go out. The model that was meant to surface sales insights is producing outputs the sales team doesn’t trust—and therefore doesn’t use. The automation that was supposed to reduce manual processing has created a new category of manual processing: fixing what the automation got wrong.
Nothing catastrophically failed. The technology did roughly what it was supposed to do. But the results don’t match the expectation. And now there’s a growing pile of disconnected systems, frustrated end users, and AI outputs that nobody is quite willing to act on without a human double-checking first.
Six months in, the organization isn’t further ahead. It’s further behind—with more complexity layered on top of the existing complexity and a leadership team that’s understandably reluctant to admit publicly that the big AI push hasn’t quite delivered.
Sound familiar? It should. It’s the story underneath a lot of the AI announcements happening right now.

Why speed without foundation doesn’t work
Here’s the engineering reality that gets lost in the boardroom conversation.
AI doesn’t operate independently of the systems underneath it. It works with whatever it’s given—your data, your processes, your workflows, and your organizational logic. And what that means in practice is that AI compounds what’s already there. The good and the bad, equally, without prejudice.
If your data is clean, consistent, and well-structured, AI finds the signal in it faster than any human team could. If your data is messy, inconsistent, and siloed across systems that don’t talk to each other, AI scales that mess. Confidently. At volume. Around the clock.
If your core processes are clearly defined and systematically followed, AI automates them reliably. If your processes are actually just a collection of individual habits and informal workarounds dressed up in process language, AI tries to automate the habits and the workarounds. And what comes out the other end doesn’t look much like what you were hoping for.
Technical debt doesn’t disappear when you deploy AI on top of it.
It multiplies.
And the faster you move, the faster it multiplies.
This is the part that’s genuinely counterintuitive about the current moment. Speed feels like the competitive variable. And in some contexts, it is. But in AI deployment, the organizations doing the quiet, unglamorous foundational work before they add the technology layer are not falling behind. They’re setting themselves up to pull ahead in a way that will be very hard to catch up with.

The companies nobody is writing press releases about
There’s a category of organization that almost never makes it into the AI success stories—because their progress doesn’t lend itself to dramatic announcements.
They’re not deploying four tools in eight weeks. They’re spending those eight weeks understanding exactly which one problem AI could solve most reliably, given the state of their current data and infrastructure. They’re having the uncomfortable internal conversations about which processes actually need to be redesigned before they can be automated. They’re auditing their data pipelines—not because it’s exciting, but because they understand that everything downstream depends on it.
They’re documenting workflows that everyone assumed were already documented. They’re retiring legacy systems instead of running new ones alongside them indefinitely. They’re building feedback mechanisms so that when AI does get deployed, there’s a way to know quickly whether it’s working—and to course-correct when it isn’t.
None of this gets a press release. None of it makes a good conference slide.
But in 18 months, when organizations that moved fast are still untangling their initial deployments, these companies will have something rare and genuinely hard to replicate—an AI foundation that actually works, connected to clean data, running on well-defined processes, with a team that trusts the outputs enough to act on them.
That’s the compounding advantage. And once it starts compounding, it’s very hard for anyone else to close the gap.

The trust problem nobody talks about enough
There’s another dimension to this that deserves more airtime than it usually gets.
When AI deployments move too fast and deliver inconsistent outputs, they create a trust problem inside the organization. And once that trust is broken, it’s genuinely hard to rebuild.
End users who’ve had poor experiences with AI tools don’t quietly update their expectations and give the next implementation a fair chance. They develop workarounds. They do the AI step and then redo it manually—because they don’t trust what came back. They start treating the AI layer as an obstacle rather than an asset. And they’re not wrong to do so. The tool hasn’t earned their confidence yet.
What this means practically is that a rushed deployment doesn’t just fail to deliver ROI. It actively makes the next deployment harder—because now you’re fighting both the technical challenges and the accumulated skepticism of a team that’s already been burned once.
Getting it right—or right enough that people trust the output—is worth far more than getting something out the door quickly. Because rebuilding trust inside an organization is slow, expensive work. And it’s entirely avoidable.

What deliberate actually looks like
I want to be specific here, because "move deliberately" can sound like "move slowly"—and that’s not what I mean.
"Deliberate" means making conscious choices about where to start, based on honest assessment rather than external pressure. It means choosing the deployment with the cleanest data, the most clearly defined process, and the most measurable outcome—not the one that makes the best story for the board pack.
It means defining what success looks like before you deploy, not after.
It means asking the questions that are slightly uncomfortable to ask. What does our data actually look like in this area? What are the manual workarounds in this process that we’ve never formally acknowledged? If this doesn’t work the way we’re expecting—what's the plan?
And it means being willing to do the foundational work first, even when that work isn’t glamorous and doesn’t have an obvious, immediate ROI attached to it. Because that work is the difference between AI that compounds your advantage and AI that compounds your problems.

The questions worth sitting with this week
Before the next vendor demo, before the next deployment decision, before the next conversation about where to push AI further—try these:

Are we moving at this pace because we’re genuinely ready or because we’re responding to pressure?
If our current AI deployment quietly failed tomorrow, what would we have actually learned?
Are we building something that compounds over time—or something that looks good in a quarterly update?
Do the people using our AI outputs actually trust them enough to act on them without double-checking?
The answers won’t always be comfortable. But they’ll be more useful than another vendor demo.

Here’s where I’ll leave you this Monday.
The organizations that define their industries over the next decade won’t be the ones that move first.
They’ll be the ones that moved smart—that did the quiet, unglamorous, foundational work while everyone else was busy making announcements.
Speed is seductive right now. The pressure is real, the noise is loud, and moving fast feels like the only responsible response to a moment that everyone keeps telling you is historic.
But the slowest thing you can do right now is rush into something your foundation isn’t ready to support.
Because unpicking a messy AI deployment—rebuilding trust with a skeptical team, untangling disconnected systems, going back to fix the data architecture that should have been addressed first—costs more in time, money, and organizational energy than taking an extra quarter to get the foundation right.
The race isn’t to deployment. It’s to sustainable, compounding advantage.
And that race is won in the preparation. Not the announcement.

Where is the pressure to move fast on AI coming from in your organization right now—and is it helping or hurting? I’d genuinely like to know.

posts.title: AI Won’t Replace Companies. It Will Expose Them.
posts.content:
Let me start with something that doesn’t get said enough in these conversations.

The executives I speak to aren’t afraid of AI. Not really. What they’re actually afraid of—if you get them off the record, away from the optimism of the all-hands meeting—is what AI might reveal about how their organization actually operates versus how they’ve always assumed it does.

That fear is more rational than it sounds. And I think it deserves a more honest conversation than it usually gets.

Here’s the thing nobody puts on the vendor slide deck.
AI doesn’t fix broken systems. It amplifies them.

I know that’s not what the pitch says. The pitch says AI will streamline your operations, surface hidden insights, and unlock productivity you didn’t know you had. And it can do all of those things—but only if the foundation underneath it is solid.

What I’ve seen, after years of building these systems in production environments, is something a little less comfortable. A company deploys an AI-powered customer service tool. Expectations are high. Within weeks, the model is confidently replicating the same bad answers that the weakest agents were giving before—except now it’s doing it at ten times the volume, at 2am, with no one watching.

The AI didn’t create the problem. The problem was already there, baked quietly into the workflows and the data. The AI just turned up the volume on it.

That’s the part that gets left out of the Monday morning briefing.

What actually gets exposed
When organizations move from pilot programs into real deployment, four things tend to surface. Not as shocking revelations—more like things everyone half-knew but nobody had formally acknowledged.

The processes that were never really processes. AI forces you to document and systematize how work actually gets done. And most organizations discover, at this point, that what they call a process was really just a collection of individual habits held together by institutional memory. Finance does it one way. Operations does it differently. Both call it the same thing. You cannot build a reliable system on that kind of ambiguity.

Decision-making that’s slower than anyone admitted. AI operates in near real-time. Organizations that require multiple sign-offs before anything meaningful can happen find that their intelligent new infrastructure is running laps around their own governance model. The bottleneck was never the technology.

Data that’s more fragmented than the IT roadmap suggested. This is the one that quietly kills the most projects. Data living in disconnected systems, inconsistently labelled, owned by different teams with different standards—no model compensates for that. The AI will only ever be as coherent as what you feed it. And most organizations, if they’re honest, have been feeding their systems a fairly inconsistent diet for years.

The gap between strategic intent and execution capacity. Plans look clean in presentations. Deployment exposes whether the organization actually has the operational muscle, the cross-functional alignment, and the willingness to retire old systems—rather than just running new ones alongside them indefinitely.

None of these are AI problems. They’re business problems that AI makes impossible to keep deferring.

But here’s where it gets genuinely interesting.
I don’t want to leave this in a purely cautionary place, because that’s not the full picture either.

The same dynamic that punishes operationally weak organizations rewards strong ones—at a scale and speed that simply wasn’t available before. And this is what I think leadership teams are underestimating, even more than the risks.

A company with clean data, clearly defined processes, and the ability to make decisions quickly doesn’t just adopt AI more smoothly than its competitors. It compounds. Every efficiency AI introduces becomes the foundation for the next one. Every insight feeds back into a system already designed to act on it.

The gap between these organizations and everyone else doesn’t grow gradually. It accelerates.

We’re entering a period where operational maturity—which has always mattered but has rarely been a source of dramatic, visible competitive advantage—is about to become the defining variable. The companies quietly doing the unglamorous work right now are building a lead that will be very hard to close in two or three years’ time, when everyone else finally realizes what they missed.

The honest question to ask yourself
I’ve started framing AI adoption less as a technology initiative and more as an organizational stress test. One that runs continuously and doesn’t particularly care about your implementation timeline.

So instead of asking, "How do we adopt AI?"—try asking this instead:

If we deployed AI honestly across our core operations today, what would it show us?

If the answer involves a lot of things you’d rather not have surfaced right now, that’s actually useful. It’s telling you exactly where to focus before you add the amplifier.

Three things worth stress-testing before anything else:

Process clarity. Can you describe, without ambiguity, how a core workflow runs from start to finish—including the exceptions, the manual workarounds, and the moments where someone just uses their judgment? If you can’t document it cleanly, you can’t automate it reliably.

Data integrity. Where does your most business-critical data actually live? Who owns it? How consistently is it structured across your systems? If the answers are vague, your AI readiness is lower than your current vendor relationships suggest.

Decision velocity. How long does it take your organization to go from a clear signal in the data to a committed action? If that’s measured in weeks, AI will surface insights that expire before anyone acts on them.

Be honest with yourself across these three. The gaps you find aren’t reasons to delay—they're your actual roadmap.

What I’d ask leadership to do differently
The most important AI decisions your organization makes over the next 18 months probably won’t involve choosing a model or a platform. They’ll involve internal readiness—and that’s a leadership responsibility, not something you can delegate to the technology team.

Fund the boring work. Data governance, process documentation, and system consolidation—none of it is exciting, none of it photographs well for the annual report, and none of it has an obvious, immediate ROI. It’s also the difference between AI that compounds your advantage and AI that compounds your problems. Protect that budget.

Own the risk trade-offs. Every AI deployment involves real decisions about speed versus accuracy, automation versus human oversight, and moving fast versus moving carefully. These are not engineering calls. They’re business calls. If your technical team is making them without explicit guidance from leadership, you have a governance gap—and eventually it will cost you.

Measure things that actually matter. Adoption rates are not a success metric. Neither is the number of prompts your team runs per week. The question is whether AI is reducing the cost of a specific unit of work, compressing a cycle time that matters, or improving a decision that has real business consequences. If you can’t connect the investment to a measurable outcome, you’re still in experiment mode—whatever the internal communications say.

So here’s where I’ll leave you this Monday.
AI isn’t arriving to sort out the things your organization has been quietly deferring. It’s going to make those things visible, urgent, and expensive to ignore.

For the companies willing to do the hard, unglamorous work of getting ready—it becomes something else entirely. Not just a cost-reduction lever or a productivity tool, but a genuine multiplier on everything that’s already working well.

The organizations that define their industries over the next decade won’t be the ones that move fastest to buy. They’ll be the ones that moved thoughtfully enough to prepare.

AI won’t transform your business overnight. But it will show you—at scale, clearly, and without much sympathy—exactly what was already holding it back.

The question is whether you’d rather find that out on your terms or the market’s.

Three questions worth taking into your week:

→ If AI exposed our three most critical workflows right now, what would it find? → Where does slow decision-making create the most drag in our organization? → Do we have one clean, trusted source of data for our most important processes—or are we working from fragments?

posts.title: Are You Automating Tasks, or Actually Building a Business?
posts.content:
The illusion of progress
We’re in a gold rush. Every week, a new vendor promises their latest AI feature will deliver "unprecedented productivity." And for anyone in a director or CXO seat, it’s a hard pitch to resist.

So licenses get purchased. A press release goes out. The organization is officially "AI-powered."
But let’s be honest with each other—buying seats isn’t a strategy. It’s an accounting entry.

What most organizations are actually doing right now is running a massive, uncoordinated productivity experiment. Throwing technology at the wall and hoping something sticks. It feels like progress. It rarely is. More often, it’s just a very expensive way of funding your own inefficiency.

Toys vs. tools—and why the difference matters
If you want to move from experimenting to actually building something institutional, you need to get clear on one distinction: what’s a toy in your organization, and what’s a tool?

The toy is what I call the Shadow AI problem. It’s the employee pasting a sensitive product roadmap into a public chatbot because it’s faster than using the approved system. They’re not being more productive—they're quietly creating a security liability that nobody has quantified yet. This is the "wild west" phase of AI adoption, and most organizations are still deep in it.

The tool is something engineered. It’s connected to your proprietary data, it behaves predictably where it needs to, and it’s built to be right at scale—not just fast. There’s a world of difference between the two, and right now, most boardrooms are funding toys while expecting tools.

The data debt nobody wants to talk about
Before we get to algorithms and models, we need to talk about something less exciting but far more important: data debt.

Here’s my reality as an AI/ML engineer—I spend roughly 80% of my time on data preparation. The actual model? That’s the last 20%. If your leadership team is waiting for the AI to magically fix your data architecture, I can tell you now how that project ends.

The hard truth is that you cannot build a modern AI system on a foundation of siloed, inconsistent, or legacy data. It simply doesn’t work.
So the question directors need to stop asking is "Why isn’t the AI performing?" The question they need to start asking is "What does our data pipeline actually look like?" The unglamorous, foundational work of data governance isn’t optional—it's the prerequisite for everything else.

Governance isn’t IT’s problem—it's yours.
AI is the first technology where the risk profile isn’t just technical. It’s ethical and legal too.

How is your organization handling personally identifiable information inside AI workflows? What happens when a model confidently generates a customer commitment that turns out to be completely wrong? These aren’t hypothetical edge cases anymore.

And here’s the part that often gets missed: Governance cannot be delegated entirely to the IT department. It belongs in the boardroom.

Defining your organization's risk tolerance for AI is a business decision—not an engineering one. Are you willing to trade accuracy for speed? That’s a trade-off leadership needs to own.

The "build vs. buy" trap
One of the most common mistakes I see—especially in organizations trying to move fast—is attempting to mirror what the big tech companies are doing without having remotely similar infrastructure.

Most companies don’t need to build a foundational AI model from scratch. What they actually need is the connective tissue—the systems that link existing models to their specific business processes, data, and workflows.

And while we’re at it, stop measuring AI success by adoption rates or number of prompts run. Those metrics tell you very little. Start measuring by cost-per-unit-of-work saved or speed-to-market improvement. If you can’t connect your AI investment to a real business outcome, you don’t have a tool yet—you have a very expensive experiment.

Three questions for your next Monday meeting
If you want to start moving from toys to tools, try these on your direct reports this week:
"How are we quantifying the ROI of our current AI initiatives—and are we measuring them against our actual KPIs?"
"What security and compliance guardrails do we have in place, and do they cover everything our teams are using today?"
"Is our data genuinely ready for AI, or are we spending most of our time cleaning up after our own tools?"

The answers will tell you exactly where you stand.
The bottom line
The organizations that define their industries over the next decade won’t be the ones that bought the most licenses.

They’ll be the ones that treated AI as a genuine strategic shift—and did the hard, unglamorous groundwork to back it up.
You don’t need more AI right now. You need more clarity.

You don’t need more experiments. You need more infrastructure.
That’s your reality check for this week.

posts.title: Boardroom AI: Monday Reality Check
posts.content:
There’s a directive echoing through boardrooms right now, and you’ve almost certainly heard it: "We need to integrate AI."

But here’s what usually happens next—a lot of nodding, a few expensive pilots, and mounting frustration with very little to show for it.

We’re drowning in AI noise. And for the directors, department heads, and CXOs actually held accountable for results, the gap between the hype and the reality has never felt wider.
I’ve spent my career as an AI/ML engineer building these systems from scratch. When I talk to leaders, the frustration isn’t usually with the technology. It’s that nobody is giving them a straight answer about what it actually takes to make it work.

So here’s why I’m starting this series.

Every Monday, I’ll be cutting through the noise with one clear, grounded insight—no technical rabbit holes, no miracle-cure promises. Just a high-signal briefing for the people responsible for the bottom line and the long game.

Risk—the hidden liabilities sitting inside your current AI roadmap
Readiness—whether your organization is actually set up for AI or needs a foundation reset first

My commitment to you is simple. By the time your first Monday meeting kicks off, you’ll have one perspective-shifting insight you can actually use—whether that’s challenging a flawed assumption or giving your team a sharper direction.

posts.title: How AI Agents Actually Work
posts.content:
Let me start with something that happened in early 2023 that I haven't been able to stop thinking about since.

A developer set up an instance of AutoGPT—one of the first publicly available AI agent frameworks—and gave it a simple goal: do research on a topic and write a summary. Straightforward enough. They stepped away.

When they came back, the agent hadn't written a summary. It had spawned subtasks. Which had spawned more subtasks. Which had spawned more. It had made dozens of API calls, consumed significant compute, and was still going—confidently, autonomously, completely lost—in a loop it had no mechanism to recognize or escape.

Nobody was harmed. No files were deleted. But the image stuck: a system given a goal, handed the tools to pursue it, and completely unable to tell that it had long since stopped making progress toward anything useful.

That's the thing about AI agents that the demos don't show you. The capability is real. The autonomy is not—at least not in the way the word implies. And understanding the difference is worth your time, because agents are about to be everywhere.

What an AI agent actually is

The word "agent" gets used so loosely right now that it's almost lost meaning. Every product seems to be announcing an agentic feature. Every AI company has agents on their roadmap. So let's get precise about what we're actually talking about.

A traditional AI chatbot does one thing: takes your input, generates a response, and stops. You write, it replies, conversation over until you write again. It has no memory of what it just said unless that's explicitly built in. It takes no actions in the world. It just produces text.

An AI agent is different in three specific ways.

It can plan. Given a goal, it breaks that goal down into steps and decides what to do in what order. It isn't just responding to your last message—it's working toward an objective across multiple actions.

It can use tools. It can browse the web, write and execute code, read and write files, send emails, call APIs, and interact with software. It can do things, not just say things.

And it loops. After taking an action, it observes the result, updates its understanding of where it is relative to the goal, and decides what to do next. This observe-plan-act cycle repeats until the goal is reached—or until something goes wrong.

That cycle—perceive, plan, act, observe, repeat—is what separates an agent from a chatbot. It's also where most of the interesting failures happen.

The mechanics: what's happening underneath

When you give an AI agent a goal, here's what's actually happening at a mechanical level.

Your goal gets passed to a large language model—the same kind of model powering ChatGPT or Claude—along with a description of the tools available to it and instructions about how to behave. The model generates a plan: a sequence of steps it thinks will achieve the goal.

Then it executes the first step. Maybe it browses a webpage. Maybe it writes some code and runs it. Maybe it searches a database. The result of that action comes back to the model as new input—"Here's what happened when you did that."

The model then generates the next step, informed by what just happened. And so on, in a loop, until it decides the goal is complete—or until it runs into something it doesn't know how to handle.

The critical thing to understand here is that every single one of these decisions is being made by a language model predicting what should come next. There is no separate planning module with real logical reasoning. There is no genuine goal representation that the system is tracking and updating. There is a very sophisticated text prediction system being asked to behave like a planner—and doing a surprisingly good impression of one, most of the time.

That distinction matters enormously when things go wrong.

The tools that make agents actually useful

The reason agents feel so different from chatbots isn't the planning—it's the tools.

When a language model can browse the web, it's not just talking about the internet. It's reading real pages, in real time, and incorporating what it finds. When it can write and execute code, it's not describing what code would do—it's running it and seeing what happens. When it can interact with APIs, it's taking real actions that have real effects.

This is what makes the demos look magical. You watch an agent receive a vague instruction, search for relevant information, write code to process it, execute that code, handle an error it encounters, try a different approach, and eventually produce a result—all without a human touching anything.

OpenAI's operator-style agents, Anthropic's Claude with tool use, Google's Project Astra, and frameworks like LangChain and AutoGPT have all demonstrated versions of this in public—and the capabilities are genuinely impressive. These aren't demos built to look good. The underlying functionality is real.

The question is what happens when the task is harder than the demo or when something unexpected occurs partway through.

Where it goes wrong—and why

Let me tell you about a few real incidents, because they're more instructive than any theoretical explanation.

AutoGPT, which launched publicly on GitHub in March 2023 and became one of the fastest-growing repositories in the platform's history according to reporting from The Verge and Wired at the time, was one of the first widely accessible agent frameworks. The early community experiences with it were revealing.

Users reported agents getting stuck in reasoning loops—deciding that in order to complete task A, they first needed to complete task B, which required task A, with no mechanism to detect or escape the circular dependency. Others reported agents making unexpected decisions about what counted as "achieving the "goal"—technically completing the stated objective in a way that completely missed the intent.

In 2023, researchers at Stanford and Google published a paper called "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior"—which demonstrated AI agents that could plan, remember, and interact with an environment convincingly. The same research community also consistently highlighted that these agents had no genuine error-detection capability. They couldn't reliably tell when they were going wrong.

More practically: early users of agent frameworks found that giving an agent access to file systems was genuinely risky. An agent trying to "clean up" a project directory might delete files it determined were unnecessary—correctly, sometimes, and catastrophically, other times. The agent wasn't malicious. It was executing what it had planned, without the judgment to recognize that its plan was wrong.

This is the core failure mode of current AI agents: they are confident executors of plans that may themselves be flawed, with limited ability to detect when the plan has gone off the rails.

The autonomy gap: what agents can't actually do

Here's the marketing version of AI agents: autonomous systems that you give a goal to and walk away from, returning to find the work done.

Here's the more accurate version: sophisticated systems that can execute multi-step tasks reliably within well-defined boundaries, that require careful human oversight for anything consequential, and that can fail in unexpected ways when they encounter situations outside their training distribution.

The gap between those two descriptions is significant.

Current agents don't have genuine situational awareness. They can't tell when they're confused in the same way a human can. They don't have a reliable internal signal that says, "I don't know how to proceed here; I should stop and ask." They have a trained tendency to keep going—to generate the next plausible action—even when the right move is to pause.

This is why the most thoughtful implementations of agent systems right now include explicit human checkpoints. Before taking irreversible actions—sending an email, making a purchase, deleting a file, calling an external API—the agent pauses and asks for confirmation. Not because the agent knows it might be wrong, but because the humans building the system know it might be wrong.

Anthropic has written publicly about this in their alignment research, describing the importance of "minimal footprint"—agents should request only necessary permissions, prefer reversible over irreversible actions, and err on the side of doing less and confirming with users when uncertain. That's not a description of autonomous capability. That's a description of careful constraint.

The myth worth killing

"AI agents are autonomous."

They aren't. Not in any meaningful sense of the word.

Autonomy implies genuine understanding of goals, reliable self-correction, and the judgment to know when to stop. Current AI agents have none of these properties in a robust way. What they have is the ability to execute sequences of actions guided by language model predictions—which looks like autonomy when the task is well-defined and goes smoothly and breaks down in revealing ways when it doesn't.

The AutoGPT loop wasn't an edge case. It was a demonstration of what happens when a system designed to keep generating next steps has no reliable mechanism for deciding that the right next step is to stop.

That doesn't make agents useless—far from it. For specific, well-scoped tasks with appropriate human oversight, they're genuinely transformative. But the gap between "useful within boundaries" and "autonomous" is wide, and it's worth knowing where current systems actually sit.

Why this is still early days

The honest assessment of AI agents in 2026 is that we're in a phase that resembles the early days of the internet—the infrastructure exists, the potential is real, and we're still figuring out what the failure modes are and how to manage them.

The frameworks are maturing fast. LangChain, AutoGPT, CrewAI, and the agent capabilities built directly into major AI platforms have all improved significantly since the chaotic early days of 2023. Human-in-the-loop checkpoints have become standard practice for consequential actions. Reliability on well-scoped tasks has genuinely improved.

But the fundamental challenge—building systems that know what they don't know, that can detect when they're off track, that have genuine judgment rather than sophisticated pattern matching—remains unsolved. And it's the kind of challenge that won't be fixed by making the underlying language model bigger or faster.

What this means for you

If you're building with agents or evaluating agent tools for your work, a few things are worth holding onto.

Scope matters more than capability. An agent given a tight, well-defined task with clear success criteria will perform dramatically better than one given a vague, open-ended goal. The impressive demos almost always involve well-scoped tasks. Keep that in mind when evaluating what you're seeing.

Irreversibility is the real risk. Actions that can be undone—drafting an email rather than sending it, creating a file rather than deleting one—are where you want agents operating until you really trust the system. The failure cases that matter are the ones you can't walk back.

Human checkpoints aren't a limitation. They're good engineers. The instinct to remove human oversight in pursuit of "full automation" is understandable but premature. The systems that work best right now are the ones that know where to pause.

And watch what happens when things go wrong, not just when they go right. The demos show you the happy path. The failure modes tell you what the system actually is.

The thing worth sitting with

AI agents are genuinely one of the most significant developments in applied AI right now. The ability to give a system a goal and have it take real actions in the world—browsing, coding, writing, communicating—is not a gimmick. The capability is real, and it's growing.

But we are in the early, messy, figure-it-out phase. The systems are impressive and unreliable in equal measure. The marketing is ahead of the reality. And the most important skill right now—for builders, for users, for anyone evaluating this technology—is being able to tell the difference between what agents can reliably do and what we're being told they can do.

The AutoGPT loop wasn't a bug. It was a preview.

The systems have improved since then. The underlying challenge hasn't gone away.

References: AutoGPT's launch and early community experiences were reported by The Verge, Wired, and TechCrunch in March-April 2023. The Stanford/Google Generative Agents paper ("Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behaviour," Park et al., 2023) is publicly available on arXiv. Anthropic's guidance on minimal footprint and safe agent design is published in their public model specification and alignment research. All incidents described are based on publicly documented community experiences and published reporting.

Next week we're cracking open another layer of AI that shapes your daily life. Follow along—and drop any systems you want torn down in the comments.

posts.title: How Google's AI Overview Works
posts.content:
---

Let me paint you a picture.
It's May 2024. Google has just rolled out AI Overviews to hundreds of millions of users across the United States. The feature has been in testing for months. The demos looked great. The internal metrics were promising. Sundar Pichai is on stage talking about the future of search.
And then the internet starts screenshotting.
Someone asks Google how to stop cheese from sliding off pizza. The AI Overview, with complete confidence and zero hesitation, suggests adding about an eighth of a cup of non-toxic glue to the sauce. The sourcing? A satirical Reddit comment from years earlier that the system had apparently absorbed and taken entirely at face value.
Someone else asks about safe rocks to eat. The overview helpfully suggests that geologists recommend eating at least one small rock per day for minerals.
These weren't edge cases buried in obscure queries. They were answers sitting at the very top of Google Search—the most visited website on the planet—presented in clean, authoritative formatting that made them look like settled fact.
Google scrambled to remove the examples. Spokespeople explained they were isolated incidents. Which they were, technically. But the incidents had already done something more lasting than embarrass the company. They had made millions of people look at that AI-generated box at the top of their search results and wonder—for the first time—whether they should actually trust it.
That question is worth answering properly. So let's open this up.

---

What AI Overview actually is
If you've used Google in the last year or so, you've seen it. You type a question, and before the blue links, before the ads, before anything else, there's a box. It has a little Google-colored sparkle icon. It contains a paragraph or two—sometimes more—that attempts to directly answer whatever you just asked.
That's an AI overview. And on the surface it seems straightforward—Google is just using AI to give you a quicker answer, right?
Sort of. But what's actually happening underneath is more complicated, more interesting, and carries more tension than the clean product experience suggests.

---

Why Google built this—and why it's complicated
To understand the AI overview, you have to understand the position Google found itself in around 2022 and 2023.
ChatGPT launched in November 2022 and within two months had over 100 million users. People were using it to get answers to questions they would previously have Googled. Microsoft announced it was integrating a version of the technology into Bing. For the first time in a long time, Google's near-total dominance of search felt genuinely threatened.
Google had its own large language model research—in fact, the transformer architecture that underpins basically every modern AI system was invented at Google. But they had been cautious about deployment, partly because of quality concerns and partly because of a tension that sits right at the heart of their business.
Here's that tension, stated plainly: Google makes money when you click on links. Advertisers pay to appear in search results. The entire revenue model depends on you going from the search results page to somewhere else on the internet.
AI Overview gives you the answer without you having to click anything.
That's not a small thing. That's Google building a feature that, if used heavily, directly competes with the mechanism that generates the vast majority of their revenue. They built it anyway—because the alternative, losing search relevance to AI-native competitors, felt more dangerous than cannibalizing their own clicks.
That context matters for understanding every design decision in the product.

---

The mechanics: what's actually happening when you search
When you type a query into Google today, the system is doing several things simultaneously that would have seemed extraordinary even five years ago.
First, your query goes through Google's traditional search infrastructure—the index of hundreds of billions of web pages that Google has been building and refining for 25 years. This part retrieves a set of relevant documents, the same way search has always worked at a basic level.
But now, those retrieved documents—or a processed version of them—get fed into a large language model alongside your original query. The model's job is to synthesise what it finds across multiple sources and generate a coherent, direct answer in natural language.
This approach has a name in the AI world: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG. The idea is to give the language model access to real, current, retrieved information rather than relying purely on what it absorbed during training. This is supposed to make it more accurate and more up-to-date than a pure language model, grounding the answer in actual sources rather than statistical patterns from training data.
In theory, this solves the hallucination problem we talked about in last week's post. The model isn't just making things up from memory—it's reading real web pages and summarizing them.
In practice, it's more complicated than that.

---

Why it still goes wrong
The glue on pizza answer is the famous one, and it's worth understanding exactly what happened there—because it illustrates a genuine limitation that RAG doesn't fully solve.
The answer came from a Reddit post on the r/Italy subreddit, where a user had jokingly suggested adding glue to pizza sauce. The post was clearly satirical in context. But Google's system, processing the text of that page as a source document, extracted the claim without extracting the context that made it obviously a joke.
This is the core problem with web-sourced AI answers: the web contains an enormous amount of content that is satirical, hypothetical, wrong, outdated, or simply not meant to be taken literally. A language model processing these pages as source material doesn't inherently understand the difference between a peer-reviewed study and a Reddit joke, between a genuine recommendation and a comedic suggestion.
The "eat rocks" incident followed similar logic. The query triggered sources that mentioned rocks in a geological or educational context, and the model synthesised those into an answer that was, to put it gently, not medically advisable.
Google has stated publicly that these examples represent a very small fraction of AI Overview responses and that the system has been updated to handle these cases better. Based on reporting from The Verge, Search Engine Land, and others who covered the incidents extensively in May and June 2024, Google removed the specific erroneous responses quickly and said it was using the incidents to improve quality filters.
That's true as far as it goes. But the underlying challenge—teaching a system to understand context, tone, and reliability across billions of web pages of wildly varying quality—isn't something a patch fully resolves.

---

What it does well
It would be unfair to write about the AI Overview without acknowledging that for a large category of queries, it works genuinely well.
Factual questions with clear, well-sourced answers—historical dates, scientific definitions, and how-to explanations for common tasks—are exactly the kind of thing AI Overview handles reliably. The synthesis across multiple sources often produces a cleaner, more useful answer than clicking through three separate links would give you.
For navigational queries—finding opening hours, checking whether a business still exists, getting a quick definition—the feature saves real time. For complex multi-part questions that would previously have required reading several articles and piecing together an answer yourself, the summarization is often genuinely helpful.
The product is not broken. For the majority of everyday queries, it works. The issue is that the majority of everyday queries is a very different thing from all queries—and users have no reliable way to know, from the presentation alone, which category they're in.

---

The thing nobody's really solved: trust signals
Here's what I find most interesting about the AI Overview from a design perspective.
When you read a traditional search result, you have signals. You can see the source—is it the NHS, or is it some blog you've never heard of? You can see how old it is. You can read the surrounding context. You make a judgment call about reliability based on information that's right there on the page.
AI Overview strips most of that away. The answer sits in a clean box with a Google logo and a sparkle icon. There are small citations underneath links to the pages it drew from, but research consistently shows that most users don't click those. They read the answer and move on.
Which means the trust signal has effectively become, Google said. And Google's brand carries enough authority that most people don't question further.
That's a significant shift in how information flows from the web to users. And it puts enormous responsibility on the quality of the underlying system—responsibility that the glue-on-pizza moment suggested the system wasn't entirely ready for.

---

The business tension, revisited
I want to come back to the revenue question because I don't think it gets enough honest discussion.
Several studies and reports published after AI Overview launched—including analyses from data firms like Similarweb and reporting from the Wall Street Journal—noted concerns from publishers and content creators that AI Overview was reducing click-through rates to their websites. If Google answers the question directly, there's less reason to visit the site that originally contained the answer.
This creates a strange dynamic where the web that Google's AI learns from gets less traffic because Google's AI answered the question. Less traffic means less incentive for publishers to create quality content. Less quality content means worse source material for AI Overview. The feedback loop points in an uncomfortable direction.
Google disputes the severity of this effect and has said that AI Overviews drive meaningful clicks to publisher sites. The honest answer is that it's probably somewhere in between—some queries drive clicks, some don't, and the net effect is something the industry is still working out.

---

What this means for you
AI Overview is useful. Use it. But treat it the way you should treat any AI-generated content—as a starting point, not a final answer.
For simple factual queries, it's probably fine. For anything consequential—medical questions, legal questions, financial decisions, anything where being wrong matters—click through to the actual sources. The citations are there for a reason.
Notice when the answer feels suspiciously clean and complete. Real answers to complex questions usually have nuance, caveats, and disagreement baked in. If the AI overview presents a complicated topic as neatly settled, that's a signal worth paying attention to.
And remember the glue. Not because Google's system is unreliable in general—it isn't. But because the most important thing to internalize about any AI system is this: confidence and accuracy are not the same thing. They never were. They never will be.

---

The summary is worth holding onto.
Google built AI Overview because it had to. The alternative-watching AI-native competitors eat into search, which was more threatening than cannibalizing some of their own clicks.
The technology underneath it—retrieval-augmented generation—is genuinely the right approach. Grounding answers in real retrieved documents is meaningfully better than pure language model generation for factual queries.
But the web is messy, contextual, and full of content that isn't meant to be taken at face value. Teaching a system to understand that at scale is hard. Progress is being made. It isn't finished.
In the meantime, the most powerful search engine ever built is also showing hundreds of millions of people AI-generated answers every day, in a format that looks authoritative, drawn from sources most of them never check.
That's worth understanding.

---

All incidents referenced in this post—including the non-toxic glue and rock-eating responses—were widely reported by major publications, including The Verge, The Guardian, BBC News, and Search Engine Land, following Google's AI Overview rollout in May 2024. This breakdown is based on publicly available information, published reporting, and industry-standard understanding of retrieval-augmented generation systems. It does not represent Google's internal architecture.
Next week we're opening up another system that shapes your daily experience in ways you haven't thought about. Follow along—and drop any systems you want properly torn down in the comments.

posts.title: Hallucinations — Why AI Confidently Lies to You
posts.content:
Let me start with something that actually happened.

In 2023, a lawyer in New York submitted a legal brief to a federal court. Solid arguments, clean formatting, six properly cited legal precedents to back it all up. The judge asked for copies of the cited cases.

The lawyer couldn’t produce them.

Because they didn’t exist. Every single case had been invented—in confident, specific, completely convincing detail—by ChatGPT. The lawyer had used the AI to help with research, trusted what came back, and never thought to check. Why would he? It read like real legal text. It had case names, court references, and dates. It sounded exactly like what it was pretending to be.

He faced sanctions. His career took a hit that will follow him for years. And the story spread everywhere—not because AI making things up was new, but because most of us had never seen the consequences land quite so hard, quite so publicly, on quite so real a person.

I think about that lawyer a lot when I use these tools. Because the terrifying part isn’t that the AI got something wrong. It’s that nothing about the output signalled that anything was wrong. It was wrong in the most dangerous possible way—confidently, fluently, and completely.

That’s a hallucination. And if you’ve spent any real time with AI tools, you’ve almost certainly run into one. You might not have caught it.

First things first—the AI wasn’t lying.

I want to clear something up before we go further, because I think the word “lying” leads people to the wrong mental model.

Lying is intentional. It requires knowing the truth and choosing to say something different. When your friend tells you they loved your cooking when they didn’t, that’s a lie. They knew. They chose.

AI systems don’t do that. They can’t do that. What they do is something stranger and, honestly, more interesting—they produce output that is completely, confidently, specifically wrong without any awareness that anything has gone wrong at all.

To understand why, you need to understand what these systems actually are underneath. And it comes down to one sentence that sounds almost too simple to matter:

Large language models don’t know things. They predict words.

That’s genuinely it. When you type a question into ChatGPT, it isn’t going away and checking a database. It isn’t retrieving verified facts from somewhere reliable. It’s doing something closer to an incredibly sophisticated, almost eerie form of autocomplete—predicting, one word at a time, what should probably come next based on everything it was trained on.

Trained on hundreds of billions of words of human text, these systems develop a staggeringly detailed sense of how language works. What kinds of words follow what other kinds of words? What a confident, well-structured, authoritative answer to this type of question usually looks like.

And right there—that last part—is where things start to go wrong.

The problem with sounding confident

Think about how you talk when you’re not sure about something.

You hedge. You say “I think” or “if I remember right” or “you might want to double-check this.” Your uncertainty leaks into your language naturally, without you even deciding to let it.

AI systems don’t have that. They have probabilities—internal calculations about what word is most likely to come next. But those probabilities don’t show up in how they write. A model can generate a completely fabricated fact with the exact same calm, clear, well-structured prose it uses when it’s accurately telling you something true.

It doesn’t know the difference between those two situations. It genuinely cannot feel the difference. It’s just producing the most plausible-sounding continuation of the conversation—and a confident, specific, detailed answer is usually more plausible-sounding than a vague, uncertain one, because that’s what good writing looks like in the training data.

So it sounds certain. Not because it checked. Not because it knows. Because certainty is the pattern it learned from the billions of words it absorbed.

That’s the trap. And it’s a deeply uncomfortable one once you really sit with it.

What’s actually happening under the hood?

Let me try to make this concrete without drowning you in technical language.

When a language model trains, it reads an almost incomprehensible amount of text and learns the relationships between ideas, words, and concepts. But it doesn’t store facts the way your phone stores a contact. There’s no clean record somewhere that says "Fact X is true; file it here.” Instead, everything gets compressed into billions of numerical parameters—a vast, tangled statistical map of how language and ideas relate to each other.

When you ask it something, it’s not looking up an answer. It’s reconstructing one—building a response that fits the shape of what a good answer to this kind of question usually looks like.

Most of the time, honestly, this works brilliantly. The patterns are rich enough that the reconstruction is accurate. But sometimes—especially for specific details, obscure facts, recent events, or things that were barely represented in the training data—the reconstruction quietly goes off the rails. The model fills in the gap with something plausible-sounding rather than stopping to say it doesn’t actually have solid information here.

The closest human analogy I can think of is this: imagine a student who read voraciously for years but wasn’t always careful about the details. Ask them to explain a concept and they’ll blow you away. Ask them for a specific citation or an exact date, and sometimes—without realizing it, without meaning to—they'll give you something that sounds right but isn’t. Their brain pattern matched to something close and served it up as fact.

Now imagine that student never second-guesses themselves. Never pauses. Never says, "Actually, let me think about whether I’m sure about this.”

That’s the AI version. Except running at an enormous scale, producing thousands of outputs a second, for millions of people who are often trusting what comes back.

The stories that should make you pause

The lawyer is the famous one. But spend any time reading about this and you find more.

Researchers have caught AI systems inventing scientific papers—complete with convincing titles, realistic author names, and correctly formatted journal references—for research that simply doesn’t exist. Ask an AI to support an argument with evidence, and it will sometimes just manufacture the evidence to fit.

Medical AI tools have given confidently wrong information about drug dosages. Travel tools have recommended hotels that closed years ago. Customer service bots have quoted company policies the company never had. In each case, the same dynamic: fluent, specific, and confident output with no internal signal that anything is wrong.

What gets me about all of these isn’t the error itself. It’s that in most cases, nothing about how the output looked would have tipped you off. It didn’t come with a warning. It didn’t hedge or stammer. It just told you something false in the same tone it uses to tell you something true.

Here’s the uncomfortable part the industry doesn’t love to talk about.

Hallucinations aren’t going to be patched away in the next update.

I know that’s not what the marketing materials suggest. I know every AI company is working on making their systems more accurate and better calibrated. And genuinely, progress is being made—retrieval-augmented systems that ground answers in verified source documents are meaningfully more reliable for factual queries than pure language models.

But the underlying dynamic—a system that generates plausible language, sometimes producing plausible but wrong language—isn't a bug sitting somewhere in the code waiting to be fixed. It’s a consequence of the fundamental architecture. The same thing that makes these systems impressively fluent and flexible is the same thing that makes them capable of hallucinating. You can’t cleanly separate those two properties.

What companies can do, and are doing, is reduce how often it happens and make it easier to detect when it does. What they cannot honestly promise is a system that never does this—because that would require something that works in a fundamentally different way.

I think it’s worth knowing that. Not to write off AI tools—they're genuinely useful, and I use them constantly. But to calibrate your trust appropriately rather than extending it blindly.

When it’s most likely to go wrong

This is the practical bit, and I think it’s more useful than a blanket “don’t trust AI.”

Hallucinations aren’t evenly distributed. They cluster in specific situations.

Specific factual claims are riskier than general explanations. “How does compound interest work?” is safer territory than "What was the exact interest rate in this specific country in this specific year?” The model is much better at the former.

Obscure topics are riskier than well-documented ones. The more something was discussed in the training data, the more solid the patterns underlying the model’s response. Ask about something that barely appeared in training, and you’re in shakier territory.

Citations, statistics, names, and dates are the highest-risk category. These are exactly the kinds of specific, verifiable details that models are most likely to reconstruct incorrectly—and also exactly the details that sound most authoritative when they’re wrong.

And pushing the model for more detail than it actually has is a reliable way to trigger confabulation. When you keep asking for more specifics and the model doesn’t have them, it doesn’t always say so. Sometimes it just fills in.

What I actually do differently now

I still use these tools every day. But a few habits have genuinely changed.

I never trust an AI citation without checking it myself. Not because I assume it’s wrong—but because I know it might be, and the cost of not checking can be serious. If it gives me a source, I verify the source exists before I use it.

I’m more skeptical when I’m asking about specifics. General concept? I’m fairly relaxed. Specific fact, figure, or reference? I check.

And I’ve stopped letting the confident tone do the work of verification for me. The way AI writes—calm, clear, authoritative—is a product of what it learned from human text. It’s not a signal of accuracy. Sounding certain and being correct are completely different things, and the model cannot always tell you which one is happening.

That last one took me a while to internalize. The fluency is genuinely impressive. It’s easy to let it feel like evidence of reliability. It isn’t.

The thing I keep coming back to

There’s something almost philosophically strange about a system that produces language without really knowing whether what it’s saying is true.

Not strange in a scary way, necessarily. Strange in a “we built something genuinely new and we’re still figuring out what that means” way.

These tools are remarkable. The things they can do—explaining complex ideas, helping you think, writing and coding, and analyzing—are real. The capability is not an illusion.

But underneath all of it is a system that works by predicting plausible language, not by knowing true things. Sometimes those two processes lead to the same place. Sometimes they don’t. And the system itself doesn’t always know which situation it’s in.

The lawyer trusted the output without checking. That’s the mistake worth not repeating.

Use these tools. Use them a lot if they’re useful to you. But use them the way you’d use a brilliant, knowledgeable friend who occasionally misremembers things and doesn’t always realize when they’re doing it.

Trust, but verify. Especially when it matters.

This breakdown is based on publicly available information, documented real-world cases, and published research on large language model behavior. It doesn’t represent the internal architecture of any specific AI system.
