posts.title: How Instagram Reels Keeps You Scrolling
posts.content:
Be honest with yourself for a second.

How many times have you picked up your phone to “just check Instagram quickly”—and then put it down twenty, thirty, or forty minutes later with absolutely no idea where the time went? No decision to keep going. No moment where you thought, "Yes, I’ll stay a bit longer.” You just… didn’t leave.

I do this more than I’d like to admit. And for the longest time I chalked it up to laziness, or poor willpower, or just the general addictiveness of short videos. But the more I’ve learned about what’s actually running underneath Instagram Reels, the more I’ve realized—this isn’t really about willpower at all. There is a system working on you, quietly, every single time you open that app. And it is very good at its job.

Let’s talk about what it actually is.

What Instagram is really trying to do

People talk about Instagram like it’s a place to share photos and watch videos. And sure, on the surface, that’s what it looks like.

But here’s the more accurate description: Instagram is an attention business. It makes money by selling ads, and ads only work if people are looking at the screen. So the entire platform—every design decision, every engineering priority, every product meeting—ultimately comes back to one question: how do we keep people here longer?

That’s the job. Not to show you good content. Not to make you happy. To keep you watching.

Now here’s the genuinely tricky part. At any given moment, there are tens of millions of videos Instagram could show you. It has to pick one. Then another. Then another after that. And it has to get that sequence right—or right enough—that you don’t put your phone down.

That’s a hard problem. And the system built to solve it is more sophisticated than most people give it credit for.

It’s watching you while you watch it.

This is the part that genuinely surprised me when I first properly understood it.

While you’re scrolling through Reels, Instagram is tracking your behavior in extraordinary detail. And I don’t mean in a vague, general sense. I mean, it’s logging the specifics of every single interaction—including the ones you didn’t consciously make.

Did you watch that video all the way through or bail after four seconds? Did you replay it? Did you slow your scroll when it started, even if you didn’t actually stop? How long did your thumb hover before moving on? Did you visit the creator’s profile without following them?

All of that is data. All of it feeds back into the system.

The things you actively do—likes, comments, shares, saves—are the obvious signals. But honestly, those aren’t even the most useful ones. People are inconsistent about tapping buttons. But your scrolling behavior? That’s harder to fake. When you stop, even for a moment, that means something. When you blow past something in half a second, that means something too.

Instagram is building a picture of you not from what you say you like, but from how you actually behave when you think you’re just passively watching videos. That distinction matters more than it sounds.

The profile you never filled out

Over time, all those tiny signals stack up into something the system treats like a portrait of your interests. Except it’s not the interests you’d write down if someone asked. It’s more specific and more honest than that.

It’s not just “you like fitness content.” It might be that you engage with short, punchy workout videos at 7am but completely ignore the same type of content after 9pm. That you stop for travel videos when you’re sitting at your desk but scroll straight past them on weekends when you’re already out of the house. That you love self-deprecating humor from small creators but find the exact same jokes from big accounts somehow less funny.

The system doesn’t understand any of this. It doesn’t need to. It just notices the patterns and acts on them.

What’s genuinely strange about this—and slightly unsettling once you notice it—is that your feed is often a more accurate reflection of your actual behavior than your own self-description would be. We all have a version of ourselves we think we are. Instagram is tracking the version we actually are, at least in terms of what we watch at 11pm on a Tuesday.

And here’s the thing that catches people off guard: one unusual session can shift your recommendations noticeably. Watch a string of home renovation videos because your partner had the phone for an hour, and suddenly your Reels are full of bathroom tile content for the next week. The system updates fast. Sometimes faster than you’d want it to.

Every video goes through a tryout first.

Here’s something most people genuinely don’t know, and I find it fascinating from an engineering perspective.

When someone posts a new Reel, it doesn’t immediately get pushed to millions of people. It gets tested first—shown to a small initial group of users whose behavior patterns suggest they might respond to it. Could be a few hundred people, could be a few thousand. The system watches what happens.

Do they watch it through? Do they engage? Do they scroll past in two seconds?

Strong signals → wider distribution. The video gets shown to more people, then more, then more again as long as the signals hold up. Weak signals → the video quietly fades. It still exists, but the algorithm essentially stops its spread.

This is clever for a few reasons. It means a video from a creator with ten followers can genuinely go wide if it performs well—the algorithm doesn’t really care about follower count; it cares about engagement signals. It also means the feed you’re seeing has, in theory, already been filtered through a performance test. You’re not seeing everything. You’re seeing what proved itself with people like you.

The flip side is that this system is very good at amplifying what already works and very slow to surface genuinely unusual or unconventional content that might take time to find its audience. The tryout process rewards immediate engagement. Slow-burn content, things that are rewarding but not instantly gratifying, can get filtered out before it ever reaches the people who’d love it.

The feed that changes while you’re in it

Here’s the bit that I think explains why Reels feels different from just watching YouTube or scrolling through a static list.

The feed isn’t just personalized to you in general. It’s adapting to you in this session, right now, based on what you’ve been doing in the last few minutes.

Open Instagram tired after a long day and spend the first few minutes quickly scrolling past anything that requires thought—the system clocks that. It starts serving you lighter, easier content. Spend ten minutes deep in football highlights, and the system leans further into sport. Pause on three consecutive cooking videos, and suddenly there are a lot more cooking videos.

This is why the app can feel like it’s reading your mood sometimes. It’s not exactly—it can’t see your face or know what kind of day you had. But your scrolling behavior in any given session is actually a pretty decent proxy for your current state. Fast, distracted scrolling looks different from slow, engaged scrolling. The system can tell the difference, and it adjusts.

This also explains the “one more video” trap better than anything else. The feed isn’t static. It’s a moving target, constantly recalibrating toward whatever is keeping you most engaged right now. By the time you think about stopping, the next video is already queued up, and it’s already been selected to be something you’re likely to respond to.

The honest part nobody really wants to say

I want to be straight with you about something, because I think it’s important, and a lot of these explainers skip over it.

This system isn’t optimized for your well-being. It’s optimized for your attention. And those two things overlap a lot—content you genuinely enjoy does tend to hold your attention. But they’re not the same thing.

Content that makes you feel vaguely anxious can hold your attention. Content that makes you feel envious of other people’s lives can hold your attention. Content that’s mildly outrageous, or slightly provocative, or engineered to make you feel just slightly worse about yourself—all of that can hold your attention. And the system, in its current form, doesn’t distinguish between “kept watching because it was genuinely great” and “kept watching because I couldn’t look away.”

It just sees that you stayed.

I don’t say this to make Instagram sound evil. The engineers working on this system are solving genuinely hard technical problems, and they’re doing it impressively well. But understanding what the system is actually optimizing for changes how you relate to it. The feed isn’t a friendly curator trying to show you things you’ll enjoy. It’s a very sophisticated system with a very specific goal—and that goal is your time.

What I keep coming back to

Instagram Reels is a remarkable piece of engineering. The behavioral tracking, the interest modelling, the content testing, the real-time adaptation—it all adds up to something that does a very hard thing very well.

But the thing worth holding onto is this: the experience feels personal because it is personal. It’s built from your actual behavior, your real patterns, and the things you respond to, whether or not you’d admit to them. That’s what makes it so effective.

And that’s also what makes it worth understanding.

The product is the surface. The system is the advantage. And the system knows you better than you might be comfortable with.

This breakdown is based on publicly available information, observed product behavior, and industry-standard system design patterns. It doesn’t represent internal or proprietary Instagram architecture.

Next week we’re cracking open another system that shapes your daily life in ways you’ve probably never thought about. Follow along—and if there’s something you want properly torn down, drop it in the comments. I read everyone.

posts.title: How Uber Matches Riders and Drivers
posts.content:
Open the Uber app, tap “Request Ride,” and within seconds you have a driver’s name, a photo, a number plate, and an ETA. It feels instant. Almost thoughtless.

It is absolutely not.

What just happened in those few seconds involved demand forecasting, geospatial matching, real-time routing, dynamic pricing, and a continuous feedback loop—all running simultaneously, across a city full of people making completely unpredictable decisions. I think about this every time I book a ride. The app is almost insultingly simple to use. The system underneath it is anything but.

Let’s get into it.

The problem Uber is actually solving

Here’s the thing people don’t really think about: Uber isn’t matching you to a car. It’s trying to balance a live marketplace of two groups of people who want fundamentally different things.

Riders want to be picked up quickly, at a price that feels reasonable. Drivers want enough steady demand that the time spent on the road is actually worth it. These two things don’t naturally align. Demand spikes on Friday evenings. Drivers tend to cluster in neighborhoods they know. A concert ends and ten thousand people open the app at the same moment. Someone needs a ride from a quiet corner of the city at 2am.

Every technical decision Uber makes flows from one goal: take that messy, unpredictable real-world situation and bring it into balance, continuously, in real time. That’s the whole game.

Seeing the city as a grid

Before Uber can balance anything, it needs to understand what’s actually happening across a city at any given moment. And you can’t manage a city if you’re thinking about it as one big blob.

So the system breaks every city into small geographic zones—a grid of cells, each covering a few city blocks. At any moment, Uber knows how many requests are coming out of each cell, how many available drivers are in or near each cell, and critically, how both of those numbers are moving. Is demand in this area climbing? Has supply in the next zone just dropped because three drivers ended their shifts?

This sounds almost mundane when you describe it. But it’s the foundation everything else sits on. It turns an incomprehensibly complex city into something the system can actually reason about and act on in real time.

The matching engine: making a hard decision look easy

When you request a ride, something genuinely difficult happens very quickly. The system can’t just find the nearest driver and call it done—nearest on a map and nearest in terms of actual arrival time are completely different things. A driver two blocks away stuck at a bottleneck might be a far worse match than a driver six blocks away on a clear road heading in your direction already.

So the matching engine is weighing several things at once. Proximity, yes. But also estimated arrival time given live traffic. Whether the driver is fully free or just finishing another ride. Which direction they’re already moving. A driver already heading toward you is a better match than one who has to double back—even if the map distance looks worse.

And here’s the part that I find genuinely impressive: Uber isn’t solving one match at a time. It’s looking at batches of requests across a zone and trying to find the best set of matches simultaneously. Giving one great driver to one rider might leave three other riders badly served. The system tries to optimize across the whole picture, not just the individual pairing in front of it.

All of this happens in milliseconds. Because every second of delay is a second added to your wait.

Surge pricing: the part everyone hates, and why it actually works

I’ll be honest—surge pricing is genuinely annoying to experience. Opening the app and seeing a 2.4x multiplier on a rainy evening feels like being punished for needing a ride at the wrong time.

But from a systems perspective, it’s one of the more elegant solutions I’ve come across.

When demand in a zone outstrips supply, prices go up. This does two things simultaneously. Some riders see the higher price and decide to wait fifteen minutes or find another option—demand softens. Meanwhile, drivers see their earnings-per-hour climbing and either stay on the road longer or move toward that zone—supply increases. The market rebalances itself, automatically, without anyone making a manual decision.

The reverse works too. Quiet periods trigger driver incentives—bonuses for completing a certain number of rides, guaranteed minimums—to ease supply back down to a level that makes sense.

The reason surge pricing makes people so angry is that it’s most visible in the moments when you most need a ride. But it’s also exactly why a ride is available at all in those moments. Without it, the system tips out of balance, and nobody can get anything.

ETA: where the system earns or loses your trust

The estimated arrival time sitting on your screen when you book a ride is doing more work than it looks like.

It’s not a rough guess. It’s a prediction built from live traffic data, historical patterns for that specific route at that specific time of day, the driver’s current position, and the complexity of the pickup itself. Uber puts real effort into getting this right because the consequences of getting it wrong are subtle but significant.

If the app tells you four minutes and the driver shows up in nine, you’ve had a bad experience before you’ve even sat down. Do that consistently and people stop trusting the number. They start hovering anxiously instead of getting on with their day. The ETA is one of those things that only gets noticed when it’s wrong.

Routing doesn’t stop at the moment you book, either. If traffic shifts while the driver is on their way to you, the system already knows and has already recalculated. Live adjustment, not just live prediction.

This matters for drivers just as much as riders. An efficient route means less dead time, more rides completed, and better earnings. The routing engine is quietly serving both sides of the marketplace at once.

The feedback loop: how the system gets smarter

Every single ride generates a signal. Whether you cancelled before the driver arrived. Whether the driver cancelled on you. How close the actual pickup time was to the predicted one. How you rated the experience. Whether you opened the app again the following week.

All of that flows back in. Cancellation patterns teach the matching engine which pairings tend to fail—maybe certain kinds of pickups at certain hours have a high drop-off rate, so those should be weighted differently next time. ETA data refines the routing models. Ratings surface patterns that aggregate data alone might miss.

The system isn’t fixed. It’s recalibrating constantly, using what actually happened to sharpen what it predicts next time. Each ride is a service and a data point simultaneously.

This feedback loop is honestly what separates a decent marketplace from a formidable one. Getting a single match right is a tractable engineering problem. Building something that gets progressively better across millions of rides, in hundreds of cities, through wildly varying demand conditions—that's genuinely hard. And it’s where the real competitive advantage lives.

Where it breaks, because it does break

New cities are hard. A new market with a thin driver base and no historical ride data gives the system almost nothing to work with. Predictions are rougher, matching is less efficient, and the experience suffers until enough rides have happened to calibrate things properly.

Surge pricing has a fairness problem that doesn’t have a clean solution. The areas where supply is chronically low tend to be lower-income neighborhoods where residents have fewer alternatives. The mechanism optimizes for market balance, not for equitable access. Uber knows this. It’s not solved.

And genuine demand shocks—an entire stadium emptying at once, a weather event, a city-wide disruption—push the system into territory it wasn’t really designed for. ETAs become unreliable. Surge multipliers spike in ways that feel punitive. The system is technically doing exactly what it was built to do, and the experience is still awful. That tension doesn’t fully go away.

What I keep coming back to

The ride is the product. The system is the advantage.

Any well-funded team can build an app that connects riders to drivers. What took years to get right—and what’s genuinely difficult to replicate—is the optimization layer underneath. The demand forecasting, the matching logic, the pricing mechanism, the routing models, and the feedback loops that make all of it smarter over time.

That’s not the app. That’s the moat.

At its core, the whole system is solving one problem, over and over, millions of times a day: given imperfect information about where supply and demand are right now, make the best possible decision in the next few milliseconds.

Do that well enough, at a sufficient scale, and you’re not just booking rides.

You’re controlling the market.

This breakdown is based on publicly available information, observed product behavior, and industry-standard system design patterns. It doesn’t represent internal or proprietary Uber architecture.

posts.title: Netflix’s Recommendation Engine – How It Decides What You Watch Next
posts.content:
You know that feeling. You open Netflix, you’re genuinely in the mood to watch something, and twenty minutes later you’re still scrolling. Nothing looks quite right. You hover over a few things, read half a description, and somehow end up rewatching something you’ve already seen.

That experience—frustrating as it is—is the result of one of the most sophisticated recommendation systems ever built. And it’s worth understanding, because it’s not just picking shows you might like. It’s making decisions about your attention, your time, and, in a very real sense, whether you stay subscribed.

Let’s open it up.

Why recommendations are the whole business
Netflix has a simple core problem: out of thousands of titles, what should appear in front of you right now?
It sounds like a small UX question. It isn’t. Around 80% of what people watch on Netflix comes directly from a recommendation. Not searching, not browsing—a recommendation. Get it wrong consistently and people stop finding things they want to watch. They churn. They cancel. The stakes are enormous.

The problem actually breaks into three distinct challenges. First, candidate generation—taking a library of millions of titles and narrowing it down to a few hundred realistic options for you. Second, ranking—ordering those options by how likely you are to actually watch them and enjoy them. Third, the tension between familiarity and discovery—showing you things you’ll definitely like while still nudging you toward things you didn’t know you’d love.

Netflix frames this as a long-term value problem. The goal isn’t to get you to click something tonight. It’s to keep you satisfied enough that you’re still here next month.

What the engine actually knows about you
Every time you interact with Netflix, you’re generating data. Some of it is obvious—ratings, thumbs up, thumbs down, and things you add to your list. But most of it is implicit, and that’s where things get interesting.
How long you watched before stopping. Whether you finished. Whether you came back to something, you paused. What time of day do you watch? What device are you on? How long your sessions typically run. All of it feeds into the system.

From this, Netflix builds two kinds of profiles. A user embedding—essentially a numerical fingerprint of who you are as a viewer, your genre preferences, your binge patterns, and how often you finish things. And an item embedding—a fingerprint for each show or film, capturing genre, tone, cast, how fresh it is, and how similar it is to other things.

These embeddings are learned, not programmed. The system figures out the patterns itself from billions of interactions across hundreds of millions of users.

The two-stage pipeline: speed first, depth second
Here’s where the engineering gets clever. Netflix can’t run a deep, complex model across its entire library every time you open the app. That would be impossibly slow. So the system works in two stages.

Stage one is retrieval. This is the fast pass—taking thousands of titles down to a few hundred candidates in under 100 milliseconds. Simple, efficient models do this work. Item-based similarity ("people who watched this also watched that"). Collaborative filtering ("users who look like you liked this"). Embedding-based nearest neighbor search. Netflix runs several of these in parallel, each feeding a different ""lane"—Trending Now, Because You Watched, New Releases, and so on.

Stage two is ranking. Now the candidates go through something much more powerful—a deep neural network that scores each one against multiple signals simultaneously.

Will you click it? Will you actually watch it? Will you finish it? Each of these gets its own probability estimate, and they get combined into a single score that determines the order you see things in.

Training this ranking model happens on billions of real interactions. Crucially, it’s optimizing for actual watch time, not just clicks. A clickable thumbnail that leads to a disappointing show is a bad outcome by design.

The application layer—where the real engineering lives
The model is only part of the story. What I find most interesting is everything built around it.

When you look at your Netflix homepage, you’re seeing the output of a system that’s doing far more than running a ranking algorithm. Product rules determine how many items appear in each row, how much space new releases get, and how to balance movies against shows against Netflix originals. Different rows map to different retrieval channels. The ranking is optimized per slot, then aggregated into a homepage that has to feel coherent and useful rather than just algorithmically correct.

Then there’s the experimentation layer. Netflix uses a bandit-style approach to A/B testing—essentially, for a slice of users, recommendations are deliberately tweaked, and the system watches what happens to watch time, retention, and churn. This is how Netflix decides which unknown indie film deserves a push versus which proven hit should be surfaced again. It’s continuous, real-time learning about what the platform should be doing.

Cold start is another genuinely hard problem. What do you show a brand new user with no history? What do you do with a new show that nobody’s watched yet? Netflix handles this through global popularity signals and content-based matching—using what a show is to find audiences who’d likely respond to it, before there’s any behavioral data to rely on.

And then there’s latency. Recommendations have to load in under 200 milliseconds for hundreds of millions of users simultaneously. Embeddings are pre-computed and cached. Approximate nearest-neighbor search tools like FAISS make vector lookups fast enough to be practical at scale. The model accuracy you see is inseparable from the infrastructure built to serve it.

Where it breaks
No honest teardown skips this part.
The echo chamber problem is real. If the system over-optimizes for engagement, it can trap you in a narrow slice of what you’ve already shown interest in. You liked one thriller, so now your homepage is 60% thrillers, and you never discover that you’d actually love a particular documentary series.

Short-term and long-term satisfaction often pull in different directions. A provocative thumbnail gets clicks. That doesn’t mean the show was good or that the user will feel satisfied tomorrow. Netflix knows this, but measuring long-term satisfaction is genuinely hard, so the system’s incentives still skew toward what’s measurable right now.

Historical bias is baked into the data. If certain kinds of content were historically surfaced more to certain audiences, that pattern gets learned and reinforced. Netflix counters this with diversity metrics and fairness constraints in the objective functions—but it’s an ongoing battle, not a solved problem.

Myths worth clearing up
"The system knows what I like."

It doesn’t know anything, in any meaningful sense. It has identified statistical patterns—users who behaved similarly to you responded well to X, so there’s a good chance you will too. If you accidentally binge one niche genre, it might overcorrect for months.

"Recommendations are just about what’s popular."

Popularity is one signal, but watch time and completion rate matter more. A massively popular show can still rank low for you if people tend to quit it halfway through or if it’s already been pushed hard to your demographic.

"A bad recommendation means the system is broken."

The system is optimized for aggregate behavior across hundreds of millions of people. It expects to be wrong sometimes—that's built in. Some of those wrong suggestions are intentional exploration, testing whether you might like something outside your usual patterns.

"Long-term satisfaction is what Netflix actually optimizes for."

Engineers care about it. But the metrics that actually drive decisions are watch time, retention, and churn. Satisfaction is real but indirect and hard to measure cleanly—so in practice the system often behaves more like a short-term engagement engine, with longer-term well-being as a secondary consideration.

Next week: AI search engines

We’re going deep on how AI-powered search actually works—retrieval-augmented generation, how results get ranked and filtered, and the decisions that determine what you see when you type a question into a search bar.

If there’s a system you want torn down, drop it in the comments. See you next week.

posts.title: Under the Hood: AI Systems - A Weekly Look at How This AI Stuff Actually Works
posts.content:
I’ll be honest with you—I got tired of not knowing.
Not tired of AI. Tired of the gap between watching something impressive and actually understanding what just happened. You see a demo, you’re genuinely amazed, and then someone asks, "But how does it work?" and the best answer most of us have is a vague hand-wave toward "neural networks" or "it’s trained on a lot of data."

That gap bothered me enough to do something about it. So I’m starting this series.
Every week, we take one AI system or application and open it up completely. Not the marketing version. The real version—architecture, training, the messy trade-offs, and the reasons things break. The stuff that usually lives in whitepapers nobody reads or research threads that assume you already have a PhD.

The thing I actually care most about
Here’s what I haven’t seen done well anywhere and what I want this series to be known for.

Most AI explainers stop at the model. They walk you through how attention works, maybe explain backpropagation, and then wrap up. And that’s genuinely useful—but it’s half the picture at best.

What nobody talks about enough is how AI applications are actually built. Not the model sitting in a research lab. The thing someone opens on their laptop and uses every day.
How does ChatGPT decide when to search the web and when to answer from memory? What’s actually happening when GitHub Copilot streams a suggestion into your editor in under a second? How does a customer support bot maintain context across a conversation, stay on topic, and still know when it’s out of its depth?
Those questions live in the layer around the model—the orchestration, the memory systems, the retrieval pipelines, the prompt architecture, and the decisions about latency and cost and failure modes. That’s where most of the interesting engineering actually happens. And that’s where we’re going to spend a lot of our time.

What to expect each week
Every post follows a similar shape. We start with the big picture—why this system matters and what problem it’s solving. Then we get into the mechanics, with real diagrams and the equations that actually matter (not just the ones that look impressive). We look at how it’s trained, how it’s optimized, and where it tends to break.
And then—the part I’m most excited about—we look at how it becomes a real application. What does the full stack look like? What decisions did the builders have to make, and what did those decisions cost them? Where are the hard problems hiding that the demos never show you?
I’ll also include something small you can run yourself most weeks. Because reading about how diffusion models work is one thing. Watching one denoise an image step by step in a notebook you’re actually running is something else entirely.

Who I’m writing this for
Honestly? Anyone who’s curious and done with being talked down to.

If you’re an engineer who uses AI tools every day but wants to understand them at a deeper level—this is for you. If you work in product or business and you’re tired of nodding along in technical conversations you only half follow—this is for you. If you’re just someone who finds this stuff fascinating and wants to actually get it—absolutely for you.
We’ll also knock down some myths along the way, because there are a lot of them. AI doesn’t understand language in any meaningful sense—it's predicting the next most likely token, over and over, at an extraordinary scale. Bigger models aren’t automatically better—thoughtful architecture regularly beats brute-force size. And "just call the API" is rarely as simple as it sounds when you’re building something real.

One small taste before we begin
In a transformer, self-attention lets every word in a sentence look at every other word at the same time. Take: "The bank by the riverbank collapsed."
A model without self-attention might easily confuse the two meanings of "bank." With it, the presence of "river" quietly shifts the interpretation of the first "bank" toward water, not finance. The ambiguity dissolves—naturally, in parallel, across the whole sentence at once.

That moment where something clicks—that's what I’m chasing every week.
Come along.
New posts drop weekly, here on the blog and in a shorter form on LinkedIn. If there’s a system you’ve always wanted to understand properly—how Perplexity actually retrieves and ranks information, what’s really going on inside an AI coding agent, how voice models convert sound into meaning—drop it in the comments. I mean it when I say I’ll read them.

The first deep dive is coming soon.

Let’s actually understand this thing.

posts.title: Prompt Engineering, Fine-Tuning & RAG-What's the Difference and When to Use Each
posts.content:
There's a conversation I keep seeing play out in every team that starts using AI seriously.

Someone tries ChatGPT, gets a mediocre response, shrugs, and concludes the tool isn't good enough. Someone else on the same team gets a remarkable response from the exact same model. Same tool. Wildly different results.

The difference almost never comes down to the model. It comes down to how they talked to it.

Last week we covered the three main ways to adapt an AI model for your specific needs—prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and RAG. This week we're going deep on all three. Not just what they are, but how they actually work in practice, what good looks like, and—most importantly—how to decide which one your situation actually calls for.

This is one of the most immediately useful weeks in the entire series. Let's get into it.

Part One: Prompt Engineering—The Most Underrated Skill in AI

Let's start with the most common mistake people make.

Most people treat prompts like search queries. Short. Casual. Vague. "Summarise this." "Write me an email." "Explain machine learning." And then they're vaguely disappointed when the output is generic, shallow, or misses the point entirely.

That's not a failure of the model. That's a failure of the prompt.

Prompt engineering is the deliberate craft of designing your inputs to get dramatically better outputs—without changing the model at all. It sounds simple. It has more depth than most people expect. And it's almost always the right place to start before reaching for anything more complex.

Here are the techniques that actually move the needle.

Give the model a role.

The single biggest upgrade most people can make is this: tell the model who it is before you ask it anything.

Compare these two prompts:

"Explain compound interest."

versus

"You are a financial educator who specializes in explaining complex concepts to first-time investors in their 20s. Explain compound interest in a way that makes them genuinely excited about starting to invest early."

Same model. Same underlying knowledge. Completely different output. The second prompt activates a specific voice, a specific audience, and a specific goal—all before the actual question is even asked.

The role doesn't have to be elaborate. Even "You are a senior software engineer reviewing code for a junior developer" or "You are a concise, no-nonsense copywriter" is enough to meaningfully shape the response.

Be specific about what you want

Vague inputs produce vague outputs. Every single time.

Don't say "write me a summary." Say, "Write me a three-paragraph summary where the first paragraph covers the main argument, the second covers the key evidence, and the third covers the implications." Keep it under 200 words and avoid jargon."

Don't say "make this better." Say, "Rewrite this email to be more direct, cut anything that isn't essential, and make sure the core ask appears in the first two sentences."

The more specifically you describe what you want—format, length, tone, structure, what to include, what to leave out—the closer the output will be to what you actually need. This isn't about being controlling. It's about giving the model the information it needs to genuinely help you.

Use examples—this is genuinely a superpower.

One of the most powerful and underused techniques is showing the model what you want instead of trying to describe it.

In AI terminology this is called few-shot prompting"—giving the model a few examples of input-output pairs before asking it to handle the real task.

Instead of trying to articulate the tone and style you want in words, just show it:

"Here are two examples of the kind of response I'm looking for:

Q: What is inflation?
A: Inflation is when your money quietly loses value over time—the same £10 buys less than it used to. It happens when too much money is chasing too few goods.

Q: What is a recession?
A: A recession is when an economy shrinks for two quarters in a row. Businesses earn less, unemployment rises, and people tighten their belts.

Now answer in the same style: What is a bear market?"

The model now has a concrete target. The result will be far more consistent with what you actually want than any description could achieve.

Ask it to think before it answers.

For complex tasks—reasoning, analysis, math, multi-step decisions—don't ask the model to jump straight to a conclusion. Ask it to think out loud first.

This is called chain-of-thought prompting, and it dramatically improves accuracy. Instead of "what's the answer," try "think through this step by step, showing your reasoning at each stage, then give your final answer."

Why does it work? Because the model generates its response token by token. When it articulates its reasoning before arriving at a conclusion, it's essentially checking its own work as it goes. Errors that would survive a direct jump to an answer often get caught in the reasoning process.

For anything involving logic, analysis, or structured thinking—always ask for step-by-step reasoning first.

Iterate. The first response is a draft, not a final answer.

The biggest mistake people make isn't writing bad prompts. It's treating the first response as final.

A prompt is the start of a conversation. If the first response misses the mark, don't start from scratch—tell the model specifically what it got wrong and what you want different. "That's too formal—make it more conversational." "You covered X well but missed Y entirely." "The structure is right, but the tone is off—here's what I'm looking for."

Each round of specific feedback narrows the gap. After two or three iterations, you'll almost always have something genuinely useful.

Part Two: Fine-Tuning—When Prompts Aren't Enough

Prompt engineering is powerful, but it has real limits.

If you need a model to consistently match a very specific voice that's hard to describe—think a brand that's built its communication style over decades—prompting will only get you so far. If you need the model to deeply understand domain-specific terminology, workflows, and conventions that aren't well-represented in its training data, you'll hit a ceiling. And if you're running thousands of similar requests and need more consistency and efficiency, a fine-tuned model will often outperform a larger general model at lower cost.

This is where fine-tuning comes in.

Fine-tuning takes a pre-trained foundation model and trains it further on your own curated dataset. The model's internal weights actually change. It doesn't just learn to follow instructions—it internalizes patterns from your data at a deeper level.

What fine-tuning is genuinely good for:

Consistent style and voice. If you have a very specific way of communicating—a particular rhythm, vocabulary, level of formality—and you have enough examples of it, fine-tuning produces results that prompting simply can't match. The model has absorbed your style rather than being instructed to approximate it.

Domain specialization. A model fine-tuned on legal contracts and case law will outperform a general model on legal tasks because it has internalized the patterns, terminology, and conventions of that domain. The same applies to medicine, finance, engineering, customer support—any field with its own language and logic.

Efficiency at scale. A fine-tuned smaller model can often match or exceed a larger general model on a specific task—at a fraction of the cost per query. If you're running millions of similar requests, this compounds quickly.

What fine-tuning is not good for:

It doesn't give the model access to new information—it bakes in what was in your training data at a specific point in time. And it's not a quick process. Preparing good training data, running the fine-tune, and evaluating the results—it's a genuine investment. Don't reach for it until you've truly exhausted what prompt engineering can do. Most problems that feel like they need fine-tuning can actually be solved with better prompts.

Part Three: RAG — Giving AI a Memory It Can Actually Use

Of the three techniques, RAG—Retrieval Augmented Generation—is arguably having the biggest practical impact on real-world AI deployments right now. Once you understand how it works, you'll understand why.

Here's the fundamental problem it solves.

Every language model has a knowledge cutoff. It knows what was in its training data and nothing more. Ask it about something that happened last month, or about your internal company documents, or about a policy that changed last week—and it either doesn't know, or worse, confidently makes something up.

RAG solves this without retraining anything.

Here's exactly how it works:

When you send a query to a RAG-enabled system, something happens before the model ever sees your question. The system searches a knowledge base—a database of documents, FAQs, manuals, reports, whatever you've loaded in—and retrieves the most relevant pieces of information.

Those retrieved chunks are then added to the prompt, essentially saying, "Here's some relevant context—now answer the question using this." The model generates its response based on both its training and the retrieved information.

The result: a model that can answer questions about things it was never trained on. Your internal HR policies. The product launched last quarter. A research paper from last week. Legal documents specific to your organization. All of it becomes accessible—without changing a single parameter in the model.

The components under the hood:

The knowledge base—your documents, chunked into manageable pieces and stored in a vector database. A vector database doesn't store text as text—it stores documents as numerical representations called embeddings, which capture meaning rather than just keywords.

The retrieval system—when your query arrives, it's converted into an embedding too, and the system finds the document chunks whose embeddings are most semantically similar. This is a meaning-based search, not keyword matching—which is why it works even when the exact words don't overlap.

The generator—the language model itself, which takes the retrieved context and your original question and generates a grounded response.

Why RAG matters so much right now:

For most practical applications, RAG solves the problem that fine-tuning can't—current, proprietary, frequently updated information. Your knowledge base can be updated in real time. Add a document, remove an old one, update a policy—the model immediately has access to the change, because it's retrieving dynamically rather than relying on baked-in weights.

It's also more transparent. Because the model is working from retrieved documents, you can often see exactly which sources informed its response—which matters enormously when you need to verify what the AI told you and where it got it from.

How to Choose—A Practical Framework

Here's how I'd think through it every time:

Start with prompt engineering. Always. It's free and fast, and you'll be surprised how far it takes you. Give the model a clear role. Be specific. Use examples. Ask for step-by-step reasoning. Iterate on the response. If you're getting 80% of the way there, that's often genuinely enough for most use cases.

Move to RAG when your problem is about information—the model doesn't know your specific data, internal documents, or recent updates. RAG connects the model's capabilities to your knowledge base without rebuilding anything.

Consider fine-tuning when you've got a very specific style or domain that can't be captured in prompts, when you're running the same type of task at real scale, or when you want a smaller and faster model to perform at the level of a larger one for your specific task.

Combine all three when you're building something serious—fine-tune for domain behavior and consistent voice, RAG for current and proprietary knowledge, and sharp prompts to tie everything together cleanly in deployment.

The mistake most people make is reaching for complexity first. Fine-tuning sounds impressive. Building a RAG pipeline sounds like proper engineering. But if a better prompt would have solved the problem, you've spent a lot of time and money on something you didn't need.

Start simple. Scale up only when the situation genuinely demands it.

This Week's Mini Challenge 🎯

Take any task you regularly use AI for and deliberately apply three of today's techniques to it:

Give the model a specific role before asking anything.
Add one or two concrete examples of the output you want.
Ask it to think through the problem step by step before giving a final answer.

Then compare the output to what you'd normally get with your usual prompt.

Drop your before and after in the comments. The difference tends to be more striking than people expect—and seeing it once is usually enough to make these habits stick.

Coming Up Next Week 👀

Week 8: The Honest Truth About LLMs — Hallucinations, Costs, and the Limits Nobody Talks About

The capabilities are real. So are the limitations. Next week we go through all of them honestly—because understanding where AI falls short is just as important as understanding what it can do.

Subscribe so you're there for it.

Seven weeks in. You now have the practical toolkit to get genuinely good outputs from AI—not by hoping, but by knowing exactly what levers to pull. That's a different kind of capability entirely. 🚀

— Beginner's AI Blueprint | New post every week.

posts.title: From Language Models to LLMs—How These Things Are Actually Built
posts.content:
Week 6—From “huh?” to “I built that.”

Last week we cracked open the engine room of generative AI. You learned that at its core, a language model is predicting the next token—over and over, building a response word by word—and that this deceptively simple process, done at an enormous scale, produces something that can reason, write, code, and converse.

But here’s the question that should be sitting in the back of your mind:

How do you actually build one of these things?

Not in the “gather a team of PhDs and a few hundred million dollars” sense—although that’s also true. I mean, what are the actual stages? What decisions get made? What does the process look like from raw data to the thing you type into on your phone?

That’s what this week is about. And it connects to something equally important: once you understand how LLMs are built, you start to understand how to use them well—and when to reach for different tools entirely.

Let’s get into it.

Stage One: Pre-Training—Building the Foundation
Everything starts with pre-training. And pre-training is, at its heart, a self-supervised learning process—which is worth understanding properly because it’s one of the cleverest ideas in modern AI.

Here’s the problem it solves.

Supervised learning—the approach we covered in Week 2—requires labelled data. You need thousands of examples where someone has already provided the correct answer. A photo labelled “cat.” An email labelled “spam.” A medical scan labelled “malignant.” Generating those labels is expensive, slow, and fundamentally limited by how much human time you can throw at it.

Training an LLM the traditional supervised way would be impossible. You can’t hire enough humans to label trillions of words of training data.

So researchers did something ingenious. They made the data label itself.

The idea is this: take a sentence—any sentence from any text. Hide the last word. Now ask the model to predict it. The hidden word is the label. You don’t need anyone to provide it. It was already there, sitting at the end of the sentence, waiting.

Do this across hundreds of billions of sentences, and you have a training process that generates its own supervision signal automatically. That’s self-supervised learning—and it’s why LLMs can be trained on essentially unlimited amounts of text without requiring any human labeling.

The model learns by doing, billions of times over:

Read context.
Predict what comes next.
Check how wrong it was.
Adjust
Repeat
By the time pre-training is done, the model has absorbed a staggering breadth of human knowledge—not by being told facts explicitly, but by learning the patterns that connect them.

What Lives Inside a Pre-Trained Model
After pre-training, what you actually have is something called a base model or foundation model. And it’s worth being precise about what that is and isn’t.

A foundation model is extraordinarily knowledgeable. It has processed more text than any human could read in thousands of lifetimes. It has a rich, nuanced understanding of language, concepts, logic, and their relationships.

But it is not, on its own, particularly useful as an assistant.

Ask a raw base model a question, and it might—quite reasonably, from its perspective—respond by generating more text that looks like the kind of text that follows questions. Which is not the same as answering them. It might complete your prompt in a way that’s technically impressive and completely unhelpful.

The base model has learned to predict text. It hasn’t learned to be helpful.

That gap is where the next stages come in.

Stage Two: Fine-Tuning—Teaching It to Actually Help
Fine-tuning is the process of taking a pre-trained base model and training it further on a much smaller, curated dataset—specifically designed to teach the model how to behave in the context you need.

For a general-purpose assistant like ChatGPT or Claude, this means training on examples of good conversations. Human-written examples of what a helpful, accurate, appropriately toned response looks like. The model already has all the knowledge it needs from pre-training. Fine-tuning is teaching it to apply that knowledge in the right way.

Think of it as the difference between someone who’s read every medical textbook ever written versus a practicing doctor. The knowledge base might be similar. The ability to translate that knowledge into a useful response to a patient—that's developed through a different kind of training.

Fine-tuning is also how you take a general-purpose model and make it domain-specific. A legal firm might fine-tune a base model on legal documents, contracts, and case law—producing a model that’s significantly better at legal tasks than a general assistant would be. A hospital might fine-tune on medical literature and clinical notes. A software company might fine-tune on their own codebase.

This is one of the most practically important concepts in modern AI deployment—because it means you don’t always have to build a model from scratch to get something that serves your specific needs.

Stage Three: Alignment—Making It Safe and Honest
Here’s a problem that fine-tuning alone doesn’t fully solve.

A model trained to produce helpful-sounding responses will sometimes produce responses that sound helpful but are actually wrong, harmful, or manipulative. Because it’s optimizing for “text that looks like good responses”—not for “responses that are actually good.”

This is where RLHF—Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback—comes in. We touched on it last week, but let’s go deeper.

RLHF works in three steps.

First, the fine-tuned model generates multiple responses to the same prompt. Then, human raters rank those responses—which one is more helpful? More accurate? More appropriate? Finally, a separate model—called a reward model—is trained to predict those human rankings. Once the reward model exists, it can evaluate responses automatically, without needing a human in the loop every time.

The main model is then trained using reinforcement learning to maximize the reward model’s score. Essentially, generate a response, get scored by the reward model, and adjust to score higher next time. Repeat until the model is reliably producing responses that humans rate as good.

The result is a model that isn’t just knowledgeable and capable of following instructions—it's aligned with human preferences for helpful, honest, and harmless behavior.

This alignment process is genuinely hard. It’s also one of the most active areas of AI research right now, because getting it wrong—producing a model that’s capable but misaligned—has real consequences.

Foundation Models — The Platforms That Everything Is Built On
Let’s talk about foundation models more specifically, because they represent something genuinely new in how AI is developed and deployed.

Download the Medium app.
Before foundation models existed, building an AI system for a specific task meant training a model from scratch on data specific to that task. You wanted to build a customer service chatbot? Train a model on customer service conversations. You wanted a code assistant? Train a model on code. Every application required a purpose-built model, built from the ground up.

Foundation models changed that entirely.

A foundation model is a large, general-purpose model trained at enormous scale—the kind of scale that only a handful of organizations in the world can afford. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and Llama—these are foundation models. They’re trained once, expensively, and then made available as a platform that others can build on.

The insight is powerful: you don’t need to understand everything from scratch to be useful in a specific context. You need a strong general foundation, plus the ability to specialize.

This is actually how human expertise works too. A specialist doesn’t start from zero—they start from a broad education and then go deep in one area. Foundation models work the same way.

Buy vs. Build—The Most Important Decision in Applied AI
Once you understand foundation models, you understand one of the most consequential decisions any organization faces when adopting AI:

Do you use someone else’s foundation model, or do you build your own?

This is genuinely not a simple question. Let’s lay out both sides honestly.

Using a foundation model (buying):

You get immediate access to state-of-the-art capability. Models like GPT-4 or Claude have been trained on more data, with more compute, and with more alignment work than almost any private organization could replicate. You can be up and running in days. The cost is per use—API calls, tokens, and usage fees.

The tradeoffs: your data goes to a third party. You have limited control over the model’s behavior. You’re dependent on the provider’s pricing, availability, and decisions. And for highly specialized domains, a general model may not perform as well as something purpose-built.

Building your own (making):

Complete control. Your data stays with you. The model can be perfectly tailored to your domain. For organizations with genuine data moats—proprietary information that nobody else has—a custom model can outperform anything available on the market.

The tradeoffs: the cost is enormous. Training a frontier model requires hundreds of millions of dollars in compute. Maintaining it is an ongoing expense. And you need a team capable of doing it—which is a significant talent constraint.

Most organizations land somewhere in the middle: use a foundation model as the base, fine-tune it on their own data, and deploy it within their own infrastructure. That hybrid approach captures most of the benefit of both options while managing the tradeoffs of each.

Three Ways to Adapt a Model—Prompt Engineering, Fine-Tuning, and RAG
When you want to make a foundation model work better for your specific use case, you broadly have three tools available. Understanding the difference between them is one of the most practically useful things in this entire series.

Prompt Engineering

The simplest tool, and often underestimated. You don’t change the model at all—you change how you talk to it.

A well-crafted prompt can dramatically improve a model’s output. Giving the model a clear role (“You are a senior financial analyst”), specific context, output format instructions, and examples of what good looks like—all of this shapes the response without touching the underlying model.

Prompt engineering is fast, cheap, and reversible. It’s almost always the right place to start. Its limitation is that it relies entirely on what’s already in the model—if the model doesn’t know something, no prompt will conjure that knowledge from thin air.

Fine-Tuning

As covered earlier, you retrain the model on your specific data. The model’s weights actually change. It learns to respond in your voice, with your terminology, with your domain knowledge baked in.

Fine-tuning is powerful for style, tone, and domain specialization. It’s more expensive and time-consuming than prompt engineering. And it still has a knowledge cutoff—whatever was in your fine-tuning data is what the model knows. It can’t look things up.

RAG—Retrieval Augmented Generation

This is where things get genuinely clever—and it’s the technique that’s exploding in practical adoption right now.

RAG doesn’t change the model at all. Instead, it gives the model access to an external knowledge base—a database of documents, FAQs, product manuals, research papers, whatever’s relevant—and retrieves the most relevant pieces of information before generating a response.

Here’s how it works in practice. You ask a question. Before the model responds, the system searches your knowledge base for relevant information. That information is added to the prompt—"here's what we found that’s relevant to this question”—and the model generates its response based on both its training and the retrieved context.

The result is a model that can answer questions about information it was never trained on. Your internal documentation. Last week’s meeting notes. A product released after the model’s training cutoff. RAG makes all of it accessible.

This is why RAG has become the dominant approach for enterprise AI deployment. It combines the language capabilities of a foundation model with the specific, current, proprietary knowledge of your organization—without the cost and complexity of fine-tuning.

How to Think About Choosing Between Them
The three approaches aren’t mutually exclusive—in practice, the most sophisticated systems use all three together. But if you’re thinking about where to start:

Start with prompt engineering. It’s free and fast, and you’ll learn a lot about what the model can and can’t do. If you’re getting 80% of the way there with good prompts, that’s often good enough.

Move to RAG when you need the model to work with specific, current, or proprietary information that isn’t in its training data. This covers the majority of real enterprise use cases.

Consider fine-tuning when you need consistent style, tone, or domain specialization that can’t be achieved through prompting—or when you need to run a smaller, faster, cheaper model that performs at the level of a larger one for your specific task.

Each tool has its place. The skill is knowing which one the situation actually calls for.

This Week’s Mini Challenge
Try the same task three different ways this week using any AI tool you have access to.

First, use a basic prompt—just ask naturally. Then, rewrite the prompt with more context, a clear role, specific instructions, and an example of what you want. Notice the difference.

That gap between your first prompt and your improved prompt? That’s prompt engineering in action. And it’s one of the most immediately useful skills in working with AI.

Drop your before and after in the comments—I'd love to see what you discover.

posts.title: The Rise of Generative AI — What It Is and How It Actually Works
posts.content:
Beginner’s AI Blueprint | Week 5 — From “huh?” to “I built that.”

November 30th, 2022. OpenAI posted a link to the internet. No big launch. No fanfare. Just a quiet “try this.”

Within five days—a million users. Within two months—a hundred million. Fastest-growing consumer app in history.

People typed a question and watched a machine respond in complete, thoughtful, almost eerily human sentences. And millions of people quietly thought the same thing:

Wait. This feels different.

It was. But not for the reason most people think.

So what actually makes generative AI different?

For four weeks, we’ve talked about AI that classifies and predicts. Spam filters label emails. Decision trees predict outcomes. Computer vision identifies objects. All useful—but they share something in common. They’re choosing between options that already exist. Given an input, they produce a label, a category, a yes or a no.

Generative AI does something fundamentally different.

It creates.

Not selecting from a menu. Not retrieving a stored answer. Actually generating something new—a paragraph, an image, a piece of code, a melody—that didn’t exist a second ago. Building it from scratch, piece by piece, based on patterns absorbed during training.

That’s the shift that makes generative AI feel so different from everything before it. And to understand how it actually works, we need to go inside the machine.

How does it generate anything at all? The prediction engine underneath

Here’s something that surprises almost everyone when they first hear it.

At its core, a language model like ChatGPT is doing one remarkably simple thing:

Predicting the next word.

That’s it. Every response you’ve ever gotten from an AI—every essay, every poem, every line of code—was produced by a model repeatedly asking itself, given everything that’s come before, what word is most likely to come next? Then it picks a word, adds it to the sequence, and asks again. And again. And again, until the response is complete.

This might sound too simple to produce anything meaningful. But consider what it actually requires to do this well.

To predict the next word accurately—across any topic, any style, any context—you have to have absorbed an enormous amount about how language works. You need to understand grammar, yes, but also logic, cause and effect, tone, personality, cultural reference, and technical knowledge. You need to know that a sentence starting “The capital of France is…” almost certainly ends with “Paris.” But also that a sentence starting “She opened the door and found…” could end a thousand different ways, and the right one depends on everything that came before it in the story.

Do this well enough, across enough domains, at enough scale—and you don’t just get a word predictor. You get something that can reason, explain, create, and converse. Not because anyone programmed it to do those things. But because all of those abilities are implicit in truly understanding language at a deep level.

That’s the magic trick. And it works because of what happens during training.

Training: where the knowledge actually comes from

Before a generative AI model can generate anything, it has to learn. And the way it learns is through a process called pre-training—exposure to a staggering amount of text.

We’re not talking about a library. We’re talking about a significant chunk of the written internet. Books, articles, Wikipedia, academic papers, code repositories, forums, and news archives. Hundreds of billions of words. Possibly trillions, for the largest models.

During pre-training, the model reads through all of this text and does one thing over and over again: it tries to predict the next word, checks how wrong it was, and adjusts its internal settings—its weights—slightly to do better next time. This is the same feedback loop we covered in Week 2, but applied at a scale that’s almost impossible to visualize.

By the end of pre-training, something remarkable has happened. The model hasn’t memorized the text—it's too much data for that, and it’s not how the process works. Instead, it has built an extraordinarily rich internal representation of how language works, what concepts mean, and how ideas connect to each other. It’s distilled patterns from an ocean of human knowledge into billions of numerical parameters.

This is why a well-trained model can discuss quantum physics and then write a limerick about your cat and then debug a Python script—all without any specific training on any of those tasks. It learned the underlying structure of human knowledge, not just a set of specific skills.

But raw pre-training isn’t enough—here's why.

Here’s a problem nobody talks about enough.

A model that’s been pre-trained on internet text has absorbed everything on the internet. Which includes a lot of things you probably don’t want an AI to reproduce. Misinformation. Toxic content. Manipulation tactics. Conspiracy theories. The full, unfiltered chaos of human online discourse.

Left alone, a pre-trained model doesn’t particularly want to be helpful. It just wants to predict the next word—which means it might continue a harmful prompt just as readily as a helpful one, because that’s what the training data suggests is statistically likely.

This is why modern models go through additional stages after pre-training.

Fine-tuning is the first. The model is trained on a curated, much smaller dataset of high-quality examples—specifically crafted to teach it what helpful, accurate, appropriate responses look like. Think of it as finishing school after a very broad education.

Then comes something called RLHF—Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Human trainers rate the model’s outputs. Good responses get positive signals, poor responses get negative ones, and the model adjusts based on that feedback. This is how a model learns not just to generate plausible text but to generate useful, safe, and honest text.

The combination of pre-training, fine-tuning, and RLHF is roughly how ChatGPT, Claude, and most modern AI assistants were built. A vast knowledge base, shaped into something actually useful.

Tokens—the real unit of AI language

You’ll hear the word “token” a lot once you start using AI APIs, and it’s worth understanding what it actually means.

Models don’t process text word by word. They process tokens—chunks of text that might be a full word, part of a word, or just punctuation. The word “unbelievable” might be split into “un,” “believ,” and “able.” A single character like “!” is its own token. Common words like “the” or “is” are single tokens.

On average, a token is roughly three-quarters of a word. So 1,000 words is approximately 1,333 tokens.

Why does this matter? Because models have a context window—a limit to how many tokens they can process at once. Think of it as working memory. Everything within the context window the model can “see” and reason about. Everything outside it, the model doesn’t know exists.

Early models had context windows of a few thousand tokens. Modern models like Claude or GPT-4 can handle hundreds of thousands. That’s why newer models can read entire documents, remember the beginning of a long conversation, and maintain coherence across much longer exchanges than their predecessors could.

The context window is one of the most important practical constraints in working with AI—and understanding it explains a lot of AI behavior that otherwise seems strange.

Temperature—why AI isn’t always predictable

Here’s something that trips people up. If the model is just predicting the next most likely word, why doesn’t it give the same answer every time you ask the same question?

Because of a setting called temperature.

When a model predicts the next token, it doesn’t just pick the single most likely option every time. It generates a probability distribution—a ranked list of possible next tokens, each with a likelihood score. Temperature controls how the model samples from that distribution.

Low temperature: the model almost always picks the most likely option. Outputs are consistent, predictable, and a bit conservative.

High temperature: the model samples more randomly from lower-probability options too. Outputs are more varied, creative, and surprising—and sometimes gloriously wrong.

This is why asking an AI to write a creative story produces something different each time, while asking it for a specific fact tends to produce more consistent answers. The task implicitly calls for different temperatures—or you can set it explicitly if you’re using an API.

Temperature is one of those settings that sounds technical but is actually very intuitive once you understand it. More randomness equals more creativity, which equals more risk.

What generative AI can and can’t do—being honest about the limits

Generative AI is genuinely remarkable. But it has real limits that are worth understanding before you rely on it for anything important.

It doesn’t know things. It predicts plausible things.

This is the root of hallucination—one of the most discussed problems in modern AI. Because the model is predicting likely next tokens based on patterns, it can produce confident-sounding text that is completely wrong. It doesn’t experience uncertainty the way you do. It just generates the most statistically plausible continuation of the prompt—and sometimes that continuation happens to be false.

It has a knowledge cutoff.

Pre-training happens at a point in time and then stops. A model trained on data up to early 2024 has no direct knowledge of anything that happened after that. It’s not connected to the internet by default. It can’t look things up. What it knows, it learned during training—and the world has moved on since then.

It doesn’t actually understand—it patterns-matches extraordinarily well.

This is a philosophical rabbit hole worth being aware of. When a model appears to reason, to empathize, to understand nuance—is it actually doing those things, or is it producing text that resembles what understanding looks like, because it was trained on human text produced by people who do understand? Researchers genuinely disagree. What’s clear is that the model is doing something powerful, even if we’re not sure exactly what to call it.

This week’s mini challenge

Use any generative AI tool this week—ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini—and deliberately test its limits. Ask it something very recent. Ask it something oddly specific. Ask it the same creative question twice and compare the answers.

Then ask yourself: where is the “next token prediction” showing through? Where can you see the seams?

Drop what you find in the comments. The more you look, the more you see.

Next week

Week 6: From language models to LLMs—the full story. Pre-training, fine-tuning, foundation models, and the difference between a language model and the thing that actually ends up in your hands. The week where the whole picture snaps into focus.

Five weeks in. You now understand not just that generative AI exists—but what’s actually happening inside it when it writes back to you. That’s a rare kind of clarity.
