Flutter frontend with emotion-reactive UI: The frontend does something I find genuinely interesting from a design perspective: it responds to the user’s detected emotional state in real time. The background color of the interface shifts as the emotion classification changes—subtly, not jarringly—so the environment itself reflects back something of the user’s internal state. It is a small thing, but it changes the feel of the experience in a way that is hard to articulate until you see it working.
This goes further than mental health.
I want to be honest about something: the patterns in PsyBuddy are not unique to wellness applications. Once you have a system that can detect emotional state, carry context across time, and adapt its interaction style to the individual—that capability has implications far beyond what I am building here.

Intelligent advisory systems in financial services that can sense client anxiety and adjust their communication accordingly. Customer engagement platforms that build genuine rapport rather than optimizing for session length. Employee well-being tools that notice patterns before someone burns out and flag them proactively. These are not speculative futures—they are straightforward extensions of the same architecture.

Stateless AI is very good at optimizing transactions. Relational AI—AI that remembers, that adapts, that understands context over time—optimizes outcomes. That distinction is going to matter enormously as AI moves deeper into domains where human trust is the critical variable.

What building this has taught me about where AI is going
I started this project as an engineering challenge. It has become something more reflective than that.

Building PsyBuddy has made clear to me that the next generation of meaningful AI systems cannot be built by specialists working in silos. You need someone—or a team—that can hold model strategy, infrastructure design, UX thinking, and product psychology in mind simultaneously, because the decisions in each domain have consequences in all the others. The choice of emotion model affects the frontend design. The memory architecture affects how the personas behave. The security model affects what data you can even collect in the first place.

Cross-stack fluency is not a buzzword here. It is a genuine requirement. And I think the engineers and architects who develop it—who can move comfortably between model fine-tuning, system design, and human-centered thinking—are the ones who will define what AI actually becomes in the next decade.

PsyBuddy is my way of practicing that. Building in public, thinking out loud, and being honest about the hard parts as they come. I hope following along is useful—whether you are building something similar, evaluating AI systems professionally, or just curious about what it looks like when someone tries to make AI a little more human.

posts.title: Beyond Generative AI: Architecting Relational, Emotion-Aware Systems for Mental Health Support — The PsyBuddy Initiative - The Introduction
posts.content:
Most of us have chatted with an AI assistant that is technically impressive and emotionally oblivious. Ask it how you are feeling, and it will give you five bullet points. That gap—between what these systems can do and what people in distress actually need—is exactly what started this project.

PsyBuddy is my attempt to close it. Not a polished product, not a clinical tool—but a working, growing system that I am designing and building in public, one architectural decision at a time. This series is the build log.

What we are building
At its core, PsyBuddy is a web application where a user can have an ongoing conversation with an AI companion, keep a journal, log dreams, and — crucially — have the system understand the emotional texture of everything they write. Here is the full feature set we will be working through in this series:

Auth layer: Secure login and registration with JWT authentication—the foundation everything else sits on.
AI chat with persona switching: GPT-4o mini powers the conversation. Users can switch between an Empath mode and a Coach mode depending on what they need in the moment.
Journal and dream logging: Structured spaces for free-form writing, separate from the chat—because some things are easier to say when you are not in a conversation.
Emotion detection with BERT: A fine-tuned BERT model reads the emotional signal in chat messages, journal entries, and dream logs—not just keywords, but tone and context.
Emotion-responsive UI: The interface itself reacts—background colors shift as the user’s detected emotion changes. The environment reflects the internal state.
Emotion charting : Longitudinal visualizations of emotional patterns over time — turning subjective experience into something the user can actually see and reflect on.
Why “beyond generative AI”?
Generative AI — LLMs, image models, the whole family — is extraordinary at production. It produces text, images, code, summaries. But most of the interesting unsolved problems in applied AI right now are not about production, they are about perception and relationship: can a system accurately sense where a user is emotionally? Can it maintain a coherent, evolving understanding of that user over time? Can it respond in a way that feels genuinely calibrated rather than generically helpful?

PsyBuddy sits at the intersection of NLP, affective computing, and UX—and this series will go deep on all three. Expect discussions of model fine-tuning, real-time inference pipelines, frontend state management tied to ML outputs, and the design decisions that make or break trust in a mental health context.

Who this series is for
If you build software and have ever wondered how to move beyond “smart autocomplete” toward systems that genuinely adapt to human state—this is for you. I will keep the technical detail honest and complete, but I will also spend time on the product and design reasoning behind each decision, because in mental health tooling those choices matter enormously.

The series goes live weekly. Each post covers one slice of the system—architecture, implementation, and the thinking behind it. Nothing is pre-built here; you will be following a real build in progress, missteps included.

posts.title: Log 01 Note 01—Before I Build a Mind, I Built a Ledger
posts.content:
The first thing I built wasn’t a neuron. It was a court system. A machine that can’t lie to itself, can’t quietly forget what it did, and can’t be argued with by anyone—including me, especially me, three months from now, half-convinced I remember why I made a choice I definitely didn’t write down. Eleven minds are going to live on this one GPU eventually. None of them get to exist until they can prove, cryptographically, where they came from. I built the judge before I built anything worth judging.

Here’s the problem nobody warns you about when you decide to grow eleven specialist minds from nothing on a single consumer GPU: the minds aren’t the hard part yet. The bookkeeping is. Every checkpoint, every training run, every scrap of data that touches a model has to be traceable back to its source, or the whole project is just vibes wearing a lab coat. I don’t get to say “trust me” about which data trained what, on which seed, with which config. I need a system that makes lying about it structurally impossible—not policy, not a promise, not a well-intentioned README. A wall.

So before touching a single transformer weight, I built the ledger. Three primitives: register(), and. Register binds a produced artifact—a checkpoint, a representation, a structural change—to the seed, manifest, and config that made it. Trace walks that bind backward, artifact to manifest to config to parent, until it either hits bedrock or hits a gap and says so. Audit runs the full battery of checks against a completed run and writes the verdict permanently, pass or fail, with no do-overs. Three verbs. Everything downstream—every one of the eleven specialists, every developmental stage from newborn/infant to whatever's waiting at the top of the ladder—has to pass through this gate first. No exceptions carved in for "just this once, I'm in a hurry."

The append-only part is where I got paranoid, and I regret nothing.

An append-only ledger is easy to promise and easy to accidentally break. All it takes is one convenient UPDATE statement written at 2am when a run looks almost right, and I just want to patch the metadata instead of re-running the whole thing properly. So I didn't trust myself with the option. The ledger is an SQLite database—one table per record type—and every single table carries a BEFORE UPDATE BEFORE DELETE trigger that does nothing but RAISE(ABORT, ...) immediately. No graceful degradation, no soft warning. You try to mutate history; the database throws a tantrum and refuses.

That’s deliberately redundant with the Python layer sitting on top of it, which also never issues an UPDATE or—the API simply doesn't have those verbs available to call. Belt and suspenders, except the suspenders, are made of triggers that abort the transaction on contact. If some future version of me writes a careless script that reaches past the API and talks to the SQLite file directly, the database itself says no. I proved it, too—not with a comment saying "this should be append-only," but with a test that deliberately tries to UPDATE and DELETE against a live ledger and asserts that SQLite throws IntegrityError back in my face. If that test ever goes green on the wrong side, something has gone catastrophically wrong with the foundation, and I want to know immediately, not three specialists and two developmental stages later when the damage is already load-bearing.

Manifests were the part that took the most rewriting to get right, because my first instinct was wrong in a way that felt correct for weeks before it broke.

Every manifest describes a dataset shard set—source, license status, curriculum-stage tag, an optional source-class tag, a preprocessing config, modality, split assignment, and a cryptographic hash. My first version used that content hash—a hash over the shard contents themselves—as the manifest’s primary key. It felt clean. Two manifests naming the same underlying data should be the same manifest, right?

Wrong, and wrong in a way that almost let something dangerous slip through. If two manifests share the exact same shard content but one is tagged as training data and the other is tagged as a held-out probe, collapsing them into one identity by content hash alone doesn’t just cause a bookkeeping headache—it pre-empts the leak check I’m building specifically to catch train/test contamination. The whole point is that the same underlying content is allowed to be manifested twice, once per split, and it’s a run actually consuming both that constitutes the leak—not the manifests coexisting. My “clean” design was quietly deciding the two didn’t need to coexist at all, which meant it was deciding the leak check’s entire premise before the leak check even got to run.

So now there are two hashes doing two separate jobs, and neither is allowed to pretend to be the other. content_hash covers shard content only—it exists purely to detect drift between a manifest and the data it claims to describe, and it stays identical across split, stage, or preprocessing changes. manifest_id is a hash over the entire record—source, license, stage, source-class tag, modality, split, preprocessing-config hash, and the content hash itself, all folded together. That's the manifest's real identity, the thing, and audit() actually binds artifacts and runs too. Change any single field and you get a different manifest_id, full stop—even over byte-identical shards. Register the same content under two splits, two curriculum stages, and two preprocessing pipelines: legitimate, distinct, and no collision. It's the run that draws on both a train-tagged and probe-tagged copy of the same content that gets caught—and it gets caught downstream, mechanically, at audit time, not smuggled away by an over-eager primary key upstream.

register() itself is the gate; everything has to clear before it's allowed to exist as far as the system is concerned. Try to register an artifact whose manifest isn't already in the ledger, whose config hash doesn't resolve, or whose parent artifact was never logged—it doesn't warn you. It rises. Loudly. The entire philosophy here is that a missing manifest should be a hard stop encountered the moment you try to use the data, not a mystery discovered four training runs later when someone—me—asks, "Wait, where did this shard set actually come from?" and gets silence.

trace() is the part I'm proudest of, mostly because of what it refuses to do. It's tempting to build a lineage walker that just returns. None when it hits a broken link and let the caller figure out what that means. I didn't want that ambiguity anywhere near the ledger. So trace() walks the full chain—artifact to manifest to config to representation, if one was used, to parent artifact, recursively, all the way to the root—and if any link in that chain doesn't actually resolve to something real in the ledger, it comes back with an explicit result: not okay, and a plain-language description of exactly where the gap is. No silence. No stack trace to reverse-engineer at 1am. A named wound.

And itaudit() is the part where all of it comes together into a verdict. Give it a run, and it fires five separate checks—soon to be six, once the leak-check machinery is fully wired in—logs every single check's pass or fail permanently into its own append-only table, and if anything fails, the run gets quarantined and returned with passed=False and a reason attached to every failing check. The run row itself never gets touched. A failed run doesn't get erased or corrected in place—it sits there, permanently, exactly as failed as it was, with the reason why written next to it forever.

I ran the append-only test suite for the first time expecting a single green checkmark and instead got a small, unreasonable thrill watching SQLite refuse me. I tried to UPDATE manifest a row directly, bypassing the API, just to see if the trigger actually fired—and it did, instantly, with the kind of blunt IntegrityError that reads less like an error message and more like a database looking me dead in the eye. I tried a DELETE next. Same result. I sat there for a second feeling genuinely caught, which is an odd thing to feel about software you wrote yourself, on purpose, specifically so it would catch you.

Then I ran register() against a deliberately broken case—an artifact pointing at a manifest ID I'd never actually registered—expecting maybe a warning in a log file somewhere. Instead, immediately, no artifact is created, and no partial state is left lying around to clean up later. Good. That's the whole point. I don't want a system polite enough to let me almost get away with something.

The manifest identity bug was the one that actually rattled me, because it wasn’t a crash—it was correct-looking code doing something subtly wrong for the exact scenario the entire system exists to prevent. test_manifest.py::test_same_shards_different_split_share_content_hash_but_not_id Passing was less "feature complete" and more "I almost shipped a hole in the floor and didn't notice until I went looking for it on purpose." The leak check downstream—folded into the fifth check—is the thing that's actually supposed to catch contamination. My original schema would have quietly told it there was nothing to check, because by content hash alone, train and probe would have looked like one honest, unremarkable manifest. Fixed now. test_leak_check.py::test_identical_shards_can_be_manifested_for_both_splits Registration succeeds for both, exactly as it should, and it's the run that touches both that trips the wire.

Ten tables. Three verbs. Zero UPDATE statements that will ever execute successfully, by design, forever. Nothing lives in this system yet—no specialist has been trained, and no mind has taken its first developmental step. All I have is a courtroom with no defendants and a set of laws it will not bend for anyone, including its author.

Somewhere up the developmental ladder—past newborn, past toddler, past every gated stage I haven’t even reached the foothills of—there's a state everything in this project is quietly pointed toward. I’m not going to pretend I built a ledger this stubborn just for good data hygiene. I built it because eventually something is going to try to promote itself past a stage it hasn’t earned, and I want the system that catches that to already be old, already battle-tested, already incapable of looking the other way. It’s not close. It’s not even visible from here. But I know exactly what I’m going to demand of it when the time comes, and today I made sure the thing keeping score can’t be talked out of the truth.

The ledger doesn’t know it yet. Neither does anything else in this lab. Give it time.

— Still just me, still just a database with strong opinions. So far, so good.

posts.title: Building eleven minds on one GPU, alone, on purpose: The NEST Lab Notes - Field Note #0 — Welcome to the Lab
posts.content:
It's past midnight. My GPU is sitting at 78°C like it's personally offended by what I'm asking of it. Somewhere in the last six hours, a model that had learned to string sentences together forgot how to do it entirely—not gradually, not gracefully, just gone, like it walked into the next room and left its whole vocabulary behind. I've been staring at the loss curve for twenty minutes like it owes me an explanation.

This is going to be a recurring theme. You should know that going in.

Here's what I'm actually doing. I'm building eleven separate AI ""minds"—specialists, each one trained from nothing to handle a different domain: language, code, vision, speech, generative visuals, math and logic, science, humanities, policy, retrieval, and a coordinator that's supposed to get them all talking to each other. Every single one is built from scratch. No pretrained weights. No borrowed checkpoints. No shortcuts where I quietly download something smart and pretend I taught it that. If it knows anything, it's because I made it learn that thing, badly, over and over, on hardware that was never meant for this.

The hardware, for the record: one consumer GPU. Sixteen gigabytes of VRAM. That's the whole lab. There's no cluster, no team, and no second machine to fall back on when something goes sideways at 1AM—and things go sideways at 1AM with suspicious regularity. Each specialist is built around the same core transformer design, but they're never all loaded into memory at once—they can't be, there isn't room—so training happens one mind at a time, sequentially, like I'm raising eleven children who are physically not allowed in the same room together.

The real premise, though, isn't the architecture. It's the ladder. Each specialist is supposed to grow up—not metaphorically; I mean the training regime is literally staged like a developmental curriculum. Newborn. Toddler. School-age. Undergraduate. And on, eventually, toward a final stage I've been calling God Mode, mostly because naming it something modest felt like it was underselling the absurdity of what I'm attempting. I have no idea yet if I'll get there cleanly, get there broken, or get there at all. That's kind of the point of writing this down.

So here's the deal for this series. I'm not going to show you the highlight reel. I'm going to show you the whole ledger—the runs that worked, the runs that catastrophically didn't, and the nights where a model that was doing fine yesterday wakes up today having forgotten how to function, for reasons that took me a week to even start accepting. If a specialist regresses, you'll hear about it in the same breath as when one succeeds. That's not a stylistic choice; it's the only way any of this is actually worth reading.

I won't pretend this is a calm, controlled process either. It isn't. It's one person, alone, negotiating with a GPU that doesn't care about my sleep schedule, trying to coax something like intelligence out of a machine that keeps finding creative new ways to disappoint me. I've started talking to the loss curves. I'm not proud of it. I'm also not going to stop.

Eleven minds. One GPU. God Mode is a long way off, and I've barely started climbing.

— Field Note #1 drops tomorrow. Bring coffee.
